cards.ev: RCT · Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2006
cards.head: T1 glottic cancer: 2.25 Gy fractions beat 2 Gy
cards.rib: Shorter RT with 2.25 Gy fractions controls more T1 glottic cancer.
cards.take: In a Japanese trial of 180 patients with T1 glottic cancer, radiotherapy in 2.25 Gy daily fractions (56.25–63 Gy over 5–5.6 weeks) was compared with 2 Gy fractions (60–66 Gy over 6–6.6 weeks). Five-year local control rose from 77% to 92%, with no extra acute or late toxicity. Slightly larger, fewer fractions should be the standard for early glottic radiotherapy.

cards.head: Low-risk thyroid cancer: skipping radioiodine is safe
cards.rib: Spare low-risk patients ablation; follow with ultrasound and Tg.
cards.take: ESTIMABL2 randomised 776 adults with low-risk differentiated thyroid cancer after total thyroidectomy to radioiodine ablation or none. At 5 years, event-free survival was 93.6% without radioiodine and 95.4% with it, within the non-inferiority margin. More patients without radioiodine had an excellent response (83% vs 76%). For low-risk disease, ultrasound and thyroglobulin follow-up can replace routine ablation.

cards.head: Sinonasal adenocarcinoma: endoscopic surgery fails less
cards.rib: Go endoscopic when the tumour can be cleared with clean margins.
cards.take: A pooled analysis of 39 studies and 1,826 patients with sinonasal adenocarcinoma compared endoscopic and open resection. Major complications occurred in 6.6% after purely endoscopic surgery versus 36.4% after open surgery, and local failure in 17.8% versus 38.5%. Open approach and advanced T stage predicted worse survival. Selection bias is likely, but in skilled hands endoscopic resection is a safe first choice.

cards.head: Most flap crises show within 24 hours; act fast
cards.rib: Watch flaps closely for 3 days; re-explore at the first warning.
cards.take: Of 1,142 free flaps at one high-volume centre, 113 (9.9%) were re-explored for poor circulation. 82% of problems appeared within 24 hours and 96% within 72 hours. Flaps that got into trouble within 72 hours were salvaged in 85%, but only 1 of 3 at one week. Flaps already abnormal on arrival in the unit did worst. Monitor closely for three days and re-explore early.

cards.head: Irradiated recipient beds quadruple flap failure odds
cards.rib: Prefer healthy vessels outside the radiation field when you can.
cards.take: A prospective study by 23 microsurgeons covering 493 free flaps found 8.3% clotted during surgery and 9.9% needed re-exploration; 4.1% failed overall. An irradiated recipient site raised failure odds 4.2-fold, and vein grafts raised postoperative clot odds 2.5-fold. Subcutaneous heparin after surgery was linked to fewer clots. Choose recipient vessels carefully in radiated necks and avoid vein grafts where possible.

rows: ≤2 cm, one lobe, no ETE, N0
>2–4 cm, one lobe, no ETE, N0
Completion only if it changes care
fig.title: ATA 2025: extent of first surgery

cards.head: ATA 2025: lobectomy first for small confined thyroid cancer
cards.rib: Offer lobectomy when DTC is confined, node-free and up to 4 cm.
cards.take: The 2025 American Thyroid Association guideline for adult differentiated thyroid cancer leans further toward less surgery. For cancer in one lobe, 2 cm or smaller, with no spread outside the gland and no nodal disease, lobectomy is recommended; for 2–4 cm tumours it can be considered. Completion thyroidectomy is no longer routinely offered but may be considered when it changes treatment or follow-up.

cards.head: Gemcitabine-cisplatin before CRT improves NPC survival
cards.rib: Offer GP induction to fit patients with advanced NPC before CRT.
cards.take: In 480 patients with locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal cancer, three cycles of gemcitabine plus cisplatin before cisplatin chemoradiation raised 3-year recurrence-free survival from 76.5% to 85.3% and overall survival from 90.3% to 94.6%. The gain came mainly from fewer distant metastases. Severe side effects were commoner (76% vs 56%), mostly low blood counts. GP induction is now a standard option.

rows: Organ-sparing surgery or RT; clear margins
Cisplatin CRT or RT; salvage TL
fig.title: ASCO larynx preservation: key calls

cards.head: Larynx preservation: choose the patient, not the protocol
cards.rib: Check voice and swallowing before choosing larynx preservation.
cards.take: ASCO's larynx preservation update says T1–T2 cancers can be treated with organ-sparing surgery or radiotherapy, but surgery must aim for clear margins rather than lean on postoperative radiotherapy. For T3–T4, cisplatin chemoradiation or radiotherapy alone saves the larynx without costing survival. Extensive T3, large T4a, cartilage breakthrough or a non-working larynx usually do better with total laryngectomy.

lines: field can reach in H&N mucosa

cards.head: Clear margins can still leave a genetically altered field
cards.rib: In follow-up, examine the whole mucosal field, not just the scar.
cards.take: Braakhuis and colleagues explained field cancerisation in genetic terms: one altered stem cell forms a small patch, which grows into a field that can exceed 7 cm and seed new tumours. In at least a third of patients, tumour-linked changes were found in normal-looking mucosa beside the cancer. Many so-called recurrences are new field tumours, so follow-up must watch the whole mucosa.

cards.head: Glowing tumour dye found the closest margin better
cards.rib: Keep frozen sections; fluorescence guidance is still in trials.
cards.take: Eighteen oral cancer patients received panitumumab-IRDye800, a dye that sticks to EGFR on cancer cells, 1–5 days before surgery. Imaging the specimen in theatre pointed to the closest margin in near-perfect agreement with final pathology (kappa 0.96 vs 0.82 for the surgeon). Fluorescence also tracked margin distance closely (R² 0.98 vs 0.75). Promising, but still an early research tool.

fig.title: Mean ICU stay after jaw flap

cards.head: Bony forearm flap matched fibula and scapula for the jaw
cards.rib: Fibula and scapula still suit larger bone and soft tissue gaps.
cards.take: A US centre compared 108 osteocutaneous radial forearm flaps with 56 fibula or scapula flaps for single-stage jaw repair. Flap survival was similar, local wound problems were fewer with the forearm, and ICU stay was shorter (4 vs 7 days). Diet, tracheostomy and dental rehab outcomes were alike. For smaller bony jaw defects, the bony forearm flap is a fair choice.

cards.head: Pre-op nivolumab plus ipilimumab gave major responses
cards.rib: Small non-randomised trial; use pre-op immunotherapy in trials.
cards.take: In the Dutch IMCISION trial, 32 patients with advanced head and neck cancer had two doses of immunotherapy before surgery. Major pathological response (90–100% tumour kill) was seen in 35% with nivolumab plus one ipilimumab dose, and 17% with nivolumab alone. No surgery was delayed in the safety phase, and no major responder relapsed at 24 months. About a third had severe immune side effects.

fig.from: Yuan, J Stomatol Oral Maxillofac Surg 2024
fig.title: Postop RT vs surgery alone, early tongue SCC

cards.head: Postop RT in early tongue cancer cut relapse, not deaths
cards.rib: Weigh RT side effects; survival gain in early tongue is unproven.
cards.take: This meta-analysis compared surgery alone with surgery plus postoperative radiotherapy in early-stage tongue cancer. Radiotherapy improved disease-free survival (OR 0.53) and freedom from locoregional relapse (OR 0.59), but overall survival did not change (HR 1.06). Data on depth of invasion alone as a reason for radiotherapy were too thin. Offer radiotherapy for clear risk features, not routinely.

cards.ev: Systematic review · Int J Oral Maxillofac Implants 2013

fig.from: Nooh, Int J Oral Maxillofac Implants 2013
fig.title: Implant survival after radiotherapy

cards.head: Implants in irradiated jaws do best in the mandible
cards.rib: Expect more losses in the irradiated maxilla; counsel patients.
cards.take: This review of 38 studies looked at dental implants in oral cancer patients given radiotherapy. Survival was 88.9% when radiation came before implants and 92.2% when after, a non-significant gap. With prior radiation, implants survived 93.3% in the mandible but only 78.9% in the maxilla, and 89.3% in free flaps. Doses above 55 Gy clearly lowered survival.

cards.head: Oral cancer rarely reaches levels IIB and V
cards.rib: Check IIA in theatre; positive IIA means clear IIB and level V.
cards.take: This prospective study examined 583 neck dissections for oral cancer. Almost all nodal spread (95.7%) sat within levels I to IV. Level IIB was involved in only 3.8% and level V in 3.3%. A positive level IIA node was the independent predictor of spread to both IIB and V. A selective I–IV dissection suits most necks; extend it when IIA is involved.

fig.title: Flap failure in jaw ORN repair

cards.head: For jaw ORN, the fibula flap fails least often
cards.rib: Plan for complications in 1 in 5 when operating on jaw ORN.
cards.take: This review pooled 19 studies with 424 free flaps used to rebuild jaws after osteoradionecrosis. About 1 in 5 patients (22.5%) had a complication after surgery. Flap failure was lowest with the fibula (3.3%) and highest with the iliac crest (11.9%). Forearm flaps had the fewest complications (13.5%), scapula the most (34.9%). Evidence is retrospective, but the fibula is a sound first choice.

lines: Deaths: surgery arm vs RT arm

cards.head: ORATOR2: TORS de-escalation arm had 2 treatment deaths
cards.rib: Small trial, but offer de-escalated RT as the safer first option.
cards.take: ORATOR2 randomised 61 patients with early p16-positive throat cancer to reduced-dose radiotherapy (60 Gy, weekly cisplatin if node-positive) or transoral surgery plus neck dissection with lighter adjuvant radiation. All 3 deaths, 2 caused by treatment (bleeding, spinal infection), and all 4 progression events occurred in the surgery arm. Swallowing scores at 1 year were similar (85.7 vs 84.7). De-escalated radiotherapy proved the safer path.

cards.head: Prior radiotherapy cut free flap success from 92% to 84%
cards.rib: Old age is no bar; prior radiation and redone joins are the risks.
cards.take: A German review of 494 head and neck flaps over ten years found 90% overall success, highest for the radial forearm flap (93%). Flaps placed after earlier radiotherapy succeeded in 83.7% versus 91.8% without, and having to redo the vessel join in theatre also predicted failure. Age did not. In irradiated necks, counsel patients about the higher risk and plan recipient vessels carefully.

cards.head: Vein grafts rescue difficult necks: 92% of flaps survive
cards.rib: Vein grafts work when vessels fall short, but wounds need care.
cards.take: In a single-centre series of 756 head and neck free flaps, 26 (3.4%) needed interposition vein grafts, more than half as a temporary arteriovenous loop. Flap survival was 92.3% with grafts versus 95.1% without, but complications were far commoner (50% vs 16.8%), mainly wound breakdown. When neck vessels are poor or out of reach, a vein graft is a reliable salvage route; watch the wounds.

fig.title: UFH infusion vs LMWH after free flaps

cards.head: Heparin drip or enoxaparin after free flaps: outcomes alike
cards.rib: Pick the heparin your unit knows; vigilance saves more flaps.
cards.take: A German review of 266 head and neck free flap patients compared low-dose unfractionated heparin infusion with daily enoxaparin after surgery. Flap survival (96.6% vs 93.3%), flap thrombosis (9.2% vs 9.5%), bleeding needing return to theatre (4.6% vs 6.7%) and haematoma were all similar. Either drug is reasonable; close monitoring and fast re-exploration matter more than which heparin you choose.

cards.head: Resected T4b buccal cancer survives almost like T4a
cards.rib: T4b: pterygoid spread and missed adjuvant therapy drive failure.
cards.take: In 277 Indian patients with cT4a or cT4b buccal and gum cancer treated with surgery then adjuvant therapy, 2-year survival was 64% for T4a and 58% for T4b, a non-significant gap. Nearly half were downstaged on pathology. In T4b, nodal extranodal spread, lateral pterygoid invasion and skipping adjuvant treatment predicted worse outcome. Operate on selected T4b, then make sure adjuvant therapy is completed.

fig.title: Scapular bone flaps by site (42 patients)

cards.head: Scapula flap: 6 of 29 maxillary flaps lost, none in the jaw
cards.rib: Great for the mandible; in the maxilla, plan hard against fistula.
cards.take: A Swedish population-based series of 42 scapular bone free flaps found a sharp split by site. Of 29 maxillary reconstructions, 6 flaps failed completely and 9 developed oronasal fistulas, although dental rehabilitation was more common. None of the 13 mandibular flaps failed. The scapula remains an excellent mandible option; for the maxilla, expect more complications and build in ways to prevent fistulas.

cards.head: Free flaps watched on the ward did as well as in ICU
cards.rib: Ward-based flap care saves ICU beds; train the ward team early.
cards.take: A single-centre US study compared 70 head and neck free flap patients monitored in intensive care with 80 moved to a general ward with less frequent flap checks. Flap failure was unchanged (2.9% vs 2.6%), as were complications, while ICU stay fell from 5.2 to 1.7 days. Rapid response calls rose from 3% to 19%. Ward monitoring works; expect more emergency calls early on.

cards.head: Virtual planning shortens surgery and cuts bone non-union
cards.rib: Mostly observational data; a 420-patient Canadian RCT is underway.
cards.take: This 2026 meta-analysis pooled 42 studies (4 randomised) of 2,763 head and neck reconstructions. Compared with free-hand shaping, virtual surgical planning cut operating time by 65 minutes, flap ischaemia by 37 minutes and hospital stay by 1.75 days. Odds of bony non-union fell (OR 0.31), as did malocclusion (OR 0.14). Flap loss, infection and plate exposure were unchanged. Practical point: plan complex jaw rebuilds virtually.

fig.title: SENT: sentinel node in T1–T2 N0 oral cancer

cards.head: Sentinel node biopsy reliably stages the N0 oral neck
cards.rib: Use it only where a trained nuclear and pathology team exists.
cards.take: In 14 European centres, 415 patients with T1–T2 oral cancer and a clinically and radiologically negative neck had sentinel node biopsy. A node was found in 99.5%, and 23% were positive and went on to neck dissection. Sensitivity was 86%, negative predictive value 95%, disease-specific survival 94%, with only 3% minor complications. Practical point: sentinel biopsy safely stages the N0 neck where expertise exists.

cards.head: Network meta-analysis: cisplatin stays the radiosensitiser
cards.rib: Fit for cisplatin? Use it; cetuximab is not a substitute.
cards.take: Pooling 44 randomised trials (13,768 patients) of drugs given with radiotherapy for locally advanced head and neck cancer, cisplatin-based regimens cut death risk most versus radiotherapy alone: weekly cisplatin by 43% (HR 0.57), three-weekly by 21% (HR 0.79). Cetuximab and added immunotherapy did not beat cisplatin chemoradiation. Weekly cisplatin had the most grade 3–4 toxicity. Practical point: cisplatin remains the backbone.

cards.head: Over 7 litres of IV fluid in surgery: 5× medical problems
cards.rib: Track fluid volume hour by hour in long free flap operations.
cards.take: Washington University reviewed 241 head and neck free flaps (1989–1998), with detailed analysis of 141. Flaps survived fully in 95%; 30-day mortality was 2.1%. Giving more than 7 litres of crystalloid during surgery independently raised major medical complications five-fold (odds ratio 5.08) and any flap complication nearly three-fold (2.75). Practical point: keep crystalloid well below 7 litres in long flap cases.

cards.head: Pedicled flaps save 3 hours and cost less than free flaps
cards.rib: Mostly retrospective data; free flaps still lead for big defects.
cards.take: This 2026 meta-analysis pooled 25 comparative studies (5,114 patients) of free versus pedicled flaps in head and neck surgery. Free flaps took 172 minutes longer and cost 1.3 to 3 times more; hospital stay did not differ. Flap failure was more frequent with free flaps; other complication differences were small. Practical point: in selected cases, a pedicled flap is a sound choice.

cards.head: Close margins in early oral cancer: adjuvant therapy helps
cards.rib: Margin status matters even when the neck is node-negative.
cards.take: An international consortium studied 1,257 patients with T1–T2N0 oral cancer. Five-year survival was 80% with clear margins but only 52% with close and 63% with positive margins. Close margins more than doubled recurrence risk. On multivariable analysis, adjuvant treatment improved outcomes in close- or positive-margin patients. Practical point: do not simply observe early oral cancer with close margins; discuss adjuvant treatment.

cards.head: Fibula jaw flaps: 1 in 4 have a complication, mostly plates
cards.rib: Plates fail more often than flaps; plan cover and fixation well.
cards.take: A 15-year review covered 117 consecutive fibula free flaps for large mandible defects, followed for about 4 years. Complications hit 26.5%: hardware failure or intolerance 13.7%, total or partial flap failure 8.5%, wound infection 2.6% and peroneal nerve injury 1.7%. Calf numbness affected 21%. Practical point: the fibula remains the workhorse for big jaw defects; watch the plate, which causes most trouble.

cards.head: Super-thin ALT matched the forearm flap, with no flap loss
cards.rib: Small retrospective study; thin ALT also spares the forearm.
cards.take: A Korean single-centre review compared 28 super-thin thigh flaps (10 mm or less) with 44 radial forearm flaps for head and neck repair. Overall complications were 7.1% versus 11.3%, not a significant gap, and fistula, reoperation and operating time were similar. Every thigh flap survived; three forearm flaps failed. When thin, pliable skin is needed, super-thin ALT is a fair forearm alternative.

fig.from: Bobdey et al., South Asian J Cancer 2018
fig.title: 5-year overall survival by stage

cards.head: Buccal cancer: 54% alive at 5 years, 43% at stage IV
cards.rib: Stage alone underplays risk; weigh nerve invasion and ENE too.
cards.take: Tata Memorial reviewed 409 surgically treated buccal mucosa cancers from 2006-2008. Overall 5-year survival was 54.1%: 85.2% for stage I, 82.9% stage II, 56.3% stage III and 42.6% stage IV. Beyond stage, comorbidity, tumour size, node status, poor differentiation, nerve invasion and extranodal spread each independently predicted death. Use these pathology features, not TNM alone, when counselling and planning adjuvant treatment.

cards.head: Compartment maxillary resection cleared 79% of deep cancers
cards.rib: Plan deep margins compartment by compartment; await longer data.
cards.take: Four referral centres reported 34 maxillary cancers reaching deep facial spaces, removed by compartment-based resection that combines endoscopic and open routes, with the template chosen from scans of the infratemporal fossa. Margins were clear in 79.4%, and back and inner margins held even with extensive fossa spread. Local control was 81.9% at one year and 75.1% at three. Promising but early, retrospective data.

cards.ev: NSQIP cohort · JAMA Facial Plast Surg 2019

fig.from: Crippen et al., JAMA Facial Plast Surg 2019
fig.title: Wound disruption after free flap

cards.head: Smoking didn't raise flap loss but doubled wound breakdown
cards.rib: Flap survival is alike, so focus extra care on smokers' wounds.
cards.take: In 2,193 US head and neck free-flap patients (NSQIP 2005-2014), 28.5% were recent smokers. Flap failure was similar: 3.3% in smokers versus 2.9% in non-smokers. But wound breakdown nearly doubled (8.8% vs 4.6%; adjusted odds 1.74), and unplanned return to theatre rose (24.8% vs 17.9%; odds 1.50). Push cessation before surgery and watch smokers' wounds closely.

cards.head: Parascapular flap fails in under 1% across 664 flaps
cards.rib: Data come mostly from small series, yet failure stays near 1%.
cards.take: A systematic review pooled 84 studies with 647 patients and 664 parascapular flaps; 73% were used in the head and neck and 43% were combined with other flaps. Pooled flap failure was 0.99%. Partial necrosis was 2.1%, venous clots 1.6%, haematoma 5.2% and wound breakdown 6.0%. The circumflex scapular system gives a dependable skin flap, on its own or combined with others.

cards.ev: Case series + review · Int Arch ORL 2017

fig.from: Brennan et al., Int Arch ORL 2017

cards.head: Temporalis flap closed 14 of 15 palate defects
cards.rib: Small series; plan temple cranioplasty now or at a later stage.
cards.take: A single-surgeon series of 15 palate defects (1-6 cm, mean 3.5 cm) repaired with the temporalis muscle flap reported 100% flap survival and successful closure in 14 (93%). Three patients had problems: two lingering fistulas and one trismus; none had facial nerve injury. One in three later needed filling of the temple hollow. A useful local option when a free flap is unsuitable.

fig.title: HBO vs no HBO before implants (1 RCT)

cards.head: HBO before implants in irradiated jaws showed no gain
cards.rib: Only one tiny trial exists; don't make HBO a routine implant step.
cards.take: A Cochrane review found just one small trial: 26 irradiated patients receiving jaw implants, half given hyperbaric oxygen. Eight implants failed in five oxygen-treated patients versus three in two controls, a non-significant difference. One treated patient developed bone necrosis and lost all implants. Denture satisfaction was similar. Evidence is very low quality, so routine hyperbaric oxygen before implants is not justified.

cards.head: Pec major flap: 1 in 4 oral repairs had some necrosis
cards.rib: Expect edge necrosis; keep pec flaps simple in high-risk cases.
cards.take: In 220 consecutive pectoralis major flaps for mouth defects, 27% developed some flap necrosis, but total loss was only 2.7% and major partial loss 9%. Flap-related complications reached 40.5%. Necrosis was likelier in women, tongue cancers, subtotal or total glossectomy, bipedicled or bone-carrying flaps, prior chemotherapy and diabetes. In such patients, keep to a plain myocutaneous design.

fig.from: Nocini et al, J Clin Med 2026

cards.head: ALT plus plate for the jaw works, but plates cause trouble
cards.rib: A fallback for frail patients; choose a bone flap when you can.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 4 studies (329 patients over 55) reviewed mandible repair with an ALT soft-tissue flap over a titanium plate instead of a bone flap. The ALT itself succeeded in 97%, with one total loss. But 28% had plate problems, plate exposure ranged from 10% to 38.7%, and infection or fistula affected 20–38.7%. Keep this for frail patients who cannot tolerate a bone flap.

cards.head: Preventing jaw ORN: no add-on has solid trial proof yet
cards.rib: Lean on pre-RT dental care and jaw-dose sparing, not add-ons.
cards.take: A Cochrane review found only 4 small trials (342 adults) testing ways to prevent jaw osteoradionecrosis after head and neck radiotherapy. Platelet-rich plasma in extraction sockets, fluoride gel versus toothpaste, and hyperbaric oxygen before implants showed no clear benefit. One 74-patient trial favoured hyperbaric oxygen over antibiotics after extractions. All evidence was very low certainty, so no add-on is proven.

cards.head: Panitumumab added to chemo did not extend survival
cards.rib: Not every anti-EGFR drug helps; skip panitumumab first line.
cards.take: SPECTRUM randomised 657 patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer to cisplatin-5FU with or without panitumumab, an anti-EGFR antibody. Median survival was 11.1 vs 9.0 months, not a significant gain (HR 0.87). Disease control lasted a little longer (5.8 vs 4.6 months). A hint of benefit in p16-negative tumours was exploratory only. Panitumumab does not replace proven first-line regimens.

fig.from: Singla et al, Indian J Plast Surg 2024
fig.title: Flap vs nearby skin temperature gap

cards.head: Thermal camera flagged failing flaps before clinical signs
cards.rib: A flap-to-skin gap over 2°C calls for a closer look at once.
cards.take: At AIIMS Jodhpur, 41 free flaps were checked with an infrared thermal camera alongside routine bedside monitoring. Healthy flaps stayed within 0.2–0.6°C of nearby skin, while the 5 compromised flaps showed gaps of about 2.4–3.3°C, appearing before clinical signs. A 2°C cut-off gave 88.6% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity. A small study, but a cheap, contact-free add-on to clinical checks.

cards.head: Tongue margins over 2.2 mm did as well as over 5 mm
cards.rib: Treat 2.2 mm, not 5 mm, as the true 'close' line in tongue.
cards.take: In 381 patients with oral tongue cancer, a 2.2 mm margin best separated those who relapsed locally from those who did not. Margins of 2.3–5 mm behaved like margins over 5 mm (HR 1.31, not significant). Margins of 0.01–2.2 mm doubled local recurrence risk (adjusted HR 2.00), and positive margins raised it almost six-fold (HR 5.73). Aim wide, but do not over-treat 3 mm.

cards.head: Vein joined within 1 cm of the IJV: 0.9% thrombosis
cards.rib: Plan pedicle length so the vein reaches the IJV or its trunk.
cards.take: This retrospective series made 246 flap venous anastomoses, 88% within 1 cm of the internal jugular vein, either end-to-side on the IJV or end-to-end on the thyrolinguofacial trunk. Only 2 veins (0.9%) clotted, and both were rescued by revision. Clots were not more frequent in irradiated or high-risk patients. Practical point: make the IJV system your first-choice outflow and join close to the main vein.

cards.head: UK survey: only 42% know a non-healing ulcer can be cancer
cards.rib: Charity survey data; ask about ulcers lasting over three weeks.
cards.take: Launching November's Mouth Cancer Action Month, the UK Oral Health Foundation reports that mouth cancer cases in England rose 119% over 20 years. Only 42% of adults recognised a non-healing ulcer as a warning sign, 59% did not know dentists check for mouth cancer, and just 31% with a possible sign sought advice. Practical point: examine mouths and ask about lingering ulcers.

cards.head: Total glossectomy, larynx kept: 91% speak clearly
cards.rib: Offer larynx-sparing glossectomy to fit, motivated patients.
cards.take: This 2023 meta-analysis pooled 642 patients whose whole tongue was removed with the voice box kept and the defect rebuilt with a flap. At about one year, 91% spoke intelligibly, 23% still needed a feeding tube and 7% a tracheostomy. A third had complications, yet major fistula and aspiration pneumonia were each about 3%. Practical point: with a bulky flap, saving the larynx is realistic.

cards.head: Fibula skin paddle: keep a muscle cuff, survival 93%
cards.rib: Small, old series, but a muscle cuff protects the skin paddle.
cards.take: Dissecting 80 cadaver legs, this landmark study showed that many lateral-leg skin perforators run through or along soleus and flexor hallucis longus, not just the septum. In 18 clinical flaps, the skin paddle survived in 33% when raised on the septum alone versus 93% with a muscle cuff. Practical point: unless septal perforators are confirmed, take a cuff of soleus and FHL with the paddle.

cards.head: About 6% of submucous fibrosis turns into cancer
cards.rib: Stop areca nut and review OSMF mouths for life; biopsy changes.
cards.take: This 2022 meta-analysis pooled studies published from 1956 to 2021 on oral submucous fibrosis. Overall, about 6% of patients developed cancer. Rates varied by population: 2% in Chinese, 6% in Taiwanese, 8% in Indian and 27% in Pakistani cohorts, though the studies differed widely. Practical point: treat OSMF as a lifelong precancer, stop areca nut, and keep regular mouth checks with biopsy of any change.

cards.head: HN005: lower-dose RT failed; 70 Gy + cisplatin stays
cards.rib: De-escalation is still experimental; keep 70 Gy with cisplatin.
cards.take: NRG-HN005 randomised 382 mostly non-smoking patients with early HPV-positive throat cancer. Standard 70 Gy with cisplatin gave 98.1% two-year progression-free survival, versus 88.6% with 60 Gy plus cisplatin and 90.3% with 60 Gy plus nivolumab. Neither lighter arm met non-inferiority, and the trial closed early. Practical point: outside trials, do not cut the radiation dose or swap out cisplatin.

fig.from: Ho et al, J Clin Oncol 2021
fig.title: Progression-free survival

cards.head: HRAS-mutant head and neck cancer: 55% respond to tipifarnib
cards.rib: Consider HRAS testing when relapsed disease runs out of options.
cards.take: Patients with recurrent head and neck cancer carrying a strong HRAS gene mutation took oral tipifarnib in this phase 2 trial. Of 20 evaluable patients, 55% responded, versus about 15% expected from standard later-line therapy. Disease control lasted 5.6 months versus 3.6 months on their previous treatment, and median survival was 15.4 months. Practical point: tumour gene panels can find this rare, targetable group.

cards.head: Delhi oral cancer: over 6 months from symptom to treatment
cards.rib: Faster referral and biopsy, not patients, is the biggest fix.
cards.take: A Delhi public-hospital study interviewed about 110 newly treated oral cancer patients; two in three had stage IV disease. The median delay from first symptom to treatment was 202 days. The longest step was diagnosis (median 90 days), then starting treatment (55 days) and patient delay (14 days). Nearly half said the first health worker did not suspect cancer. Practical point: biopsy non-healing ulcers early.

cards.head: Bone flaps beat soft flaps on patient-rated jaw function
cards.rib: Soft flaps are a fallback; rebuild bone when you safely can.
cards.take: MSKCC reviewed 114 posterolateral segmental mandibulectomies rebuilt with free flaps: 90 with bone and 24 with soft tissue only. Complication rates were similar. Patients with bony flaps scored better on FACE-Q appearance, eating, smiling, speaking and swallowing. Soft flaps were chosen more often after condyle loss or with vascular disease. Practical point: when the patient is fit, restore bone even in lateral defects.

cards.head: Pre-op chemo plus immunotherapy beats immunotherapy alone
cards.rib: Deep pre-op responses come from combinations; use them in trials.
cards.take: A 2026 meta-analysis of 23 early-phase trials (751 patients) with resectable head and neck cancer compared treatments given before surgery. Major or complete pathological response pooled 66% with chemoimmunotherapy, 18% with two immunotherapy drugs and 6% with a single drug. Severe side effects ran 17%, 3% and 29%. Practical point: chemoimmunotherapy gives the deepest responses, but phase 3 trials must confirm benefit.

fig.from: Ding et al, J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2019
fig.title: Elective dissection vs observation (N0)

cards.head: Elective neck dissection cuts N0 neck relapse to a quarter
cards.rib: Watching an N0 neck needs a clear reason and reliable follow-up.
cards.take: Pooling 6 prospective studies (5 randomised; 865 patients) of early oral cancer with a clinically negative neck, elective neck dissection lowered neck recurrence (risk ratio 0.27), all recurrences (0.53) and deaths from neck relapse (0.35) compared with watchful waiting. Benefit was clearest for tongue and floor-of-mouth cancers. Overall evidence quality was low. Practical point: offer elective dissection for early tongue and floor-of-mouth cancers.

fig.title: PORT vs none in pT1-2N1 oral cancer

cards.head: pT1-2N1: PORT helps most when few neck nodes were removed
cards.rib: Count the nodes: a small yield in pN1 tips the balance to PORT.
cards.take: Using US SEER data, 238 propensity-matched patients with pT1-2N1 oral cancer and no adverse nodal features were compared with and without postoperative radiotherapy. Overall, PORT did not improve cancer-specific survival (HR 0.80, not significant). When 16 or fewer nodes were examined, PORT was linked to better survival (adjusted HR 0.56); above 16, no gain. Practical point: a low nodal yield argues for PORT.

cards.head: Half of head and neck free flap patients have a complication
cards.rib: Fix anaemia and keep fluids lean in long free flap operations.
cards.take: Toronto reviewed 185 patients after free flap reconstruction for head and neck cancer: 53% had a complication and 40% a major one. Older age, higher ASA grade and smoking predicted major problems, and crystalloid volume predicted medical complications. Tracheostomy, low preoperative haemoglobin and prior radiotherapy predicted surgical ones. Practical point: correct anaemia, stop smoking and avoid fluid overload.

cards.head: Autofluorescence spots 89% of oral lesions; biopsy decides
cards.rib: Treat a suspicious glow as a prompt to biopsy, not a diagnosis.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 24 studies (2,761 lesions) tested autofluorescence lights for finding oral cancer and precancer. Pooled sensitivity was 89% and specificity 80%. Used alone, specificity fell to 62%, so many harmless patches look suspicious; adding scoring algorithms raised it to 95%. Most studies were done in specialist clinics. Practical point: use the light as an aid, never instead of a biopsy.

fig.from: de Geus et al, Oral Oncol 2026
rows: Dry mouth, opening, speech, social eating
fig.title: Worst-scoring domains after maxillary flaps

cards.head: After maxillary free flaps, function suffers more than mood
cards.rib: Set eating and jaw-opening rehab goals before maxillectomy.
cards.take: A 2026 meta-analysis of 7 studies (196 patients) measured quality of life after free flap repair of maxillary defects. Function took the biggest hit: dry mouth, mouth opening, speech, chewing and social eating scored worst, along with appearance. Pain, social contact and cancer worry were less affected. One study favoured virtual planning. Practical point: counsel on eating and mouth opening, and start trismus therapy early.

fig.from: Rajagopal et al, J Maxillofac Oral Surg 2026
fig.title: Radial forearm vs pec major for tongue

cards.head: Forearm flap edges pec major for tongue speech and swallow
cards.rib: Data are weak; pec major still serves unfit or salvage patients.
cards.take: A 2026 meta-analysis pooled 6 retrospective studies (380 patients) comparing radial forearm free flaps with pec major flaps after tongue cancer surgery. Speech and swallowing trended better with the forearm flap, but not significantly overall. For hemiglossectomy defects the gain was significant, though studies varied widely. Complications also looked lower. Practical point: prefer a thin free flap for hemiglossectomy; pec major stays a sound backup.

fig.title: Recipient options in a vessel-challenged neck

cards.head: Most 'vessel-depleted' necks still have usable vessels
cards.rib: Re-explore the same side before grafts or chest vessels.
cards.take: Chang Gung surgeons pooled 56 reports and their own experience of over 10,000 microvascular head and neck repairs. Even after several operations, same-side transverse cervical, superior thyroid or facial vessels usually still worked. Opposite-neck vessels or vein grafts were needed in under 20% of cases. They suggest the term 'vessel-challenged neck'. Explore the neck carefully before jumping to distant recipients.

cards.head: Buccal cancer is aggressive even when it starts small
cards.rib: Small cheek cancers still need full surgery and close follow-up.
cards.take: MD Anderson followed 119 untreated buccal cancer patients over two decades. Five-year survival was only 78% for T1 and 66% for T2 tumours, worse stage for stage than other mouth sites. Muscle invasion, Stensen duct involvement and nodal extracapsular spread lowered survival. Recurrence after radiotherapy was rarely salvaged by surgery. Treat early buccal cancer firmly: wide surgery first, with a low threshold for adjuvant treatment.

cards.head: Higher BMI means a thicker ALT flap; plan for it
cards.rib: Measure thigh fat on imaging before using ALT for thin defects.
cards.take: Shanghai surgeons measured thigh flap thickness on CT in 160 patients. With BMI 24 or more, the mid-flap point was 11.0 mm thick versus 9.0 mm in leaner patients, and all three points were thicker. Thickness rose steadily with BMI. Ultrasound was less consistent than CT. In heavier patients expect a bulkier ALT and plan thinning or another flap for thin defects.

cards.head: Fibula jaw flaps survive, but wound problems are common
cards.rib: Warn patients about wound and plate problems, not only flap loss.
cards.take: An Italian meta-analysis pooled 14 studies with 1,198 bony free flaps for the jaws, most of them fibulas. Total fibula flap loss was 6.1%, but other problems were frequent: wound breakdown 17.1%, fistula 10.4%, hardware trouble 10.4% and infection 9.0%. All studies were retrospective and reporting varied. Counsel patients that the flap usually lives, yet roughly one in six needs wound care.

cards.ev: Cohort · Br J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2025
cards.head: Surgery for cT4b mouth cancer: 59% alive at 5 years
cards.rib: Treat cT4b as borderline, not hopeless; plan compartment surgery.
cards.take: The Mumbai Oncology Group reviewed 218 patients with cT4b gingivobuccal cancers, all operated, some after chemotherapy first. 93 had compartmental ITF clearance when two or more high masticator structures were involved. At five years, 54% had local and neck control, 52% were disease-free and 59% were alive. Nodes, nerve spread and bone invasion predicted death. Many cT4b cancers deserve a surgical opinion, not palliation.

cards.ev: Systematic review · Ear Nose Throat J 2018
cards.head: Late flap failures mostly strike in the second week
cards.rib: Keep checking high-risk flaps to day 14; drain neck pus early.
cards.take: A Canadian review gathered 45 head and neck free flaps that failed after day 7, reported between 1990 and 2018. Of the 34 with full details, half failed between day 7 and day 14. Neck abscess and blood vessel compromise were the usual causes. Stopping flap checks early can miss these. In high-risk patients keep watching the flap, and treat infection fast, until day 14.

cards.head: Loupes work as well as the microscope for flap vessels
cards.rib: Pick magnification by comfort; results matched in this series.
cards.take: One US reconstructive surgeon performed 85 head and neck free flaps, 44 with 3.5x surgical loupes and 41 with the operating microscope. Anastomoses needed redoing in 12 cases: 5 with loupes and 7 with the microscope, a non-significant gap. Flap failure and complications did not differ. It is a small single-surgeon series, but an experienced surgeon can choose loupes when suitable.

cards.head: HPV-positive throat cancer: 58% lower risk of death
cards.rib: Check p16/HPV and pack-years before you counsel throat cancer
cards.take: In 323 patients with stage III–IV oropharyngeal cancer from the RTOG 0129 chemoradiation trial, 64% had HPV-positive tumours. Three-year survival was 82% with HPV-positive versus 57% with HPV-negative cancer. After adjusting for stage, age and smoking, HPV positivity cut the risk of death by 58%, and each extra pack-year of smoking raised it. Test HPV or p16 and record smoking before counselling or planning treatment.

cards.head: Jaw bone flaps survive alike; scapula ranks top
cards.rib: All four bone flaps are safe; let defect and donor site decide
cards.take: A network meta-analysis of 22 studies (1,513 patients) compared four bone flaps for mandible reconstruction. Survival was 97% for scapula, 96% for radial forearm, 94.5% for fibula and 93% for iliac crest, with no significant difference between them. Scapula ranked most likely to have the fewest failures, but most studies were non-randomised. Choose the flap by defect, donor site, implant plans and your own experience.

cards.head: Pre-op PD-1 drug works far better with TPF in oral cancer
cards.rib: Immunotherapy alone before surgery is weak; await phase 3 trials
cards.take: In a Chinese phase 2 trial, 68 patients with stage III–IVA oral cancer received pre-operative camrelizumab, a PD-1 drug, alone or with two cycles of TPF chemotherapy. Major pathological response was 76% with the combination versus 15% with immunotherapy alone, and 2-year event-free survival 91% versus 53%. Severe side effects rose (23% vs 6%) but surgery was not delayed. Promising; phase 3 proof is needed.

fig.title: Mucosal margin tools: negative predictive value

cards.head: Iodine and NBI map mucosal margins; autofluorescence lags
cards.rib: Cheap Lugol's iodine can guide mucosal cuts; still send frozens
cards.take: A systematic review screened over 19,000 records but found only eight sound studies of in-theatre tools for marking oral cancer mucosal margins. Iodine staining had negative predictive values of 92–99% and picked up dysplasia better than white light (96% vs 68% in one study). Narrow-band imaging reached 86–100%; autofluorescence 61–100%, with no margin gain. Lugol's iodine is a cheap, sensible aid, though evidence remains thin.

cards.head: TAX 323: TPF induction beat PF for unresectable cancer
cards.rib: When induction chemo is used, add docetaxel and watch neutrophils
cards.take: EORTC 24971/TAX 323 randomised 358 patients with unresectable head and neck cancer to induction cisplatin-5FU with or without docetaxel, followed by radiotherapy. Adding docetaxel (TPF) lengthened median progression-free survival from 8.2 to 11.0 months and overall survival from 14.5 to 18.8 months, a 27% lower risk of death. TPF caused more neutropenia but less mucositis and vomiting. If induction is chosen, use TPF, not PF.

cards.head: Lingual node spread flags hidden neck nodes in tongue cancer
cards.rib: Send lingual nodes separately; a positive one means a riskier neck
cards.take: In 317 patients with early (cT1–2N0) tongue cancer, 43 (14%) had cancer in lingual lymph nodes, the small nodes between the tongue and the neck. Of these, 47% also had hidden neck nodes, versus 25% of the rest. Five-year disease-specific survival was 51% with positive lingual nodes versus 84% with no lingual nodes. Look for these nodes; a positive one marks a high-risk neck.

cards.head: 1 in 9 free flap patients become delirious after surgery
cards.rib: Flag older, smoking, long-surgery cases for delirium prevention.
cards.take: In 515 head and neck free flap patients at Ohio State, 10.9% developed postoperative delirium. Risk rose with age, male sex, each extra hour of surgery, advanced neck disease and current smoking (odds about 7 times). Patients who had stopped alcohol before surgery had much lower odds (OR 0.24). Screen for these factors and start prevention steps early.

cards.head: After PORT for mouth cancer, 1 in 5 jaws develop ORN
cards.rib: Get smokers to quit; ask planners to trim jaw V60 after surgery.
cards.take: In 227 oral cavity cancer patients given postoperative IMRT and disease-free beyond a year, jaw ORN reached 15.9% at 3 years and 19.8% at 5 years. Smoking doubled the risk (HR 2.13), and risk rose with each extra percent of jaw getting 60 Gy. Active smokers with 40% or more of the jaw at 60 Gy had 29% ORN by one year.

fig.from: Zhang et al, J Surg Oncol 2024
fig.title: Median flap size

cards.head: Forearm or thigh flap: tongue outcomes come out equal
cards.rib: Match the flap to defect size; both give similar tongue results.
cards.take: This MSK review compared 54 radial forearm and 24 ALT flaps for glossectomy defects. ALT flaps were larger and more often used after mandibulotomy (50% vs 7%) and base of tongue resection (58% vs 24%). Despite tougher defects, readmission, reoperation, tube use, function and FACE-Q quality of life were similar. Choose the forearm for thin defects, ALT for bulk.

cards.head: First pembrolizumab biosimilar filed with US FDA
cards.rib: Company-reported data; cheaper pembrolizumab may follow approval.
cards.take: Samsung Bioepis filed its Keytruda biosimilar SB27 with the US FDA on 30 October, covering 18 indications including head and neck cancer. The company reports matching drug levels in a 163-patient phase 1 trial and equivalence in a 555-patient phase 3, with full phase 3 data not yet public. Biosimilars could widen access to immunotherapy as patents expire.

cards.ev: Case series · J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2021

lines: with fixed teeth at fibula surgery

cards.head: Teeth on the fibula in one sitting: 92 of 95 implants held
cards.rib: Small series; consider same-day teeth in fit, selected patients.
cards.take: This US series placed implants and a fixed bridge on the fibula during the cancer or reconstruction operation in 22 patients. Of 95 implants, 92 integrated at 9 to 15 months, about 93%. All 36 implants sitting next to skin paddles also integrated, and prosthesis work did not delay surgery. Same-day fixed teeth are realistic in carefully selected patients.

Superficial temporal, angular, contralateral facial, transverse cervical
