fig.title: Recipient vessel ladder in a depleted neck

cards.head: Vessel-depleted neck: work outward from the field
cards.rib: Plan a stepwise vessel ladder before you open a hostile neck.
cards.take: This 2024 review sums up a rare problem where evidence comes mostly from small single-centre series. Usable vessels inside the treated neck work reliably and should be sought first. If none exist, short incisions reach the superficial temporal, angular, opposite facial or transverse cervical vessels. Next come internal mammary vessels. Short pedicles can be bridged with vein grafts, AV loops or flow-through flaps.

cards.head: Clear-margin pT3N0 oral cancer still gains from PORT
cards.rib: Offer PORT for pT3 oral cancer even when margins are clear.
cards.take: This US national database study looked at 571 patients with pT3N0 oral cavity cancer, clear margins and no other adverse features. Only 31% got postoperative radiotherapy. Two-year survival was 87% with radiotherapy versus 78% without, and the gain held after propensity matching (HR 0.62). It is registry data, not a trial, but it supports offering PORT for T3 tumours.

cards.head: Laser Doppler flagged flap trouble hours before signs
cards.rib: Continuous flow sensors can buy time, but still check the flap.
cards.take: This prospective study fixed a continuous laser Doppler flow sensor to free flaps, mostly head and neck, in 71 patients; 69 gave usable traces. Flow problems appeared in 9 flaps (13%): 5 arterial and 4 venous. The device showed falling perfusion hours before clinical signs. Weak points were sensor detachment and noise early after surgery and during transfers.

cards.head: Venous flow coupler caught every failing flap
cards.rib: Venous signal flags clots early; confirm every alarm at bedside.
cards.take: In 120 head and neck free flaps watched with both a venous flow coupler and an implantable arterial Doppler, 11 needed re-exploration, 10 for vein clots. The flow coupler lost signal in all 11 (sensitivity 100%), while the arterial probe flagged only one (9.1%). Coupler false alarms ran at 13.6% and fell with experience; 9 of 11 flaps were saved. Monitor the vein, confirm clinically.

cards.head: India carries 81% of South-East Asia's oral cancer burden
cards.rib: Screen tobacco and areca users first; that is where cases are.
cards.take: A GLOBOCAN 2022 analysis counted 143,759 new oral cancers and 79,979 deaths in India, about one in ten of all cancers. Men made up 75% of cases (15.6 vs 5.0 per 100,000 in women). India holds 68% of the region's people but 81% of its oral cancer, with incidence a third above the regional average. Tobacco and areca drive most cases: screen users first.

fig.title: Masticator space surgery: gains and costs

cards.head: ITF compartment surgery cures some T4b, at a real cost
cards.rib: Select infranotch cases and plan trach and feeding tube upfront.
cards.take: A 2024 review of compartmental surgery for T4b mouth cancer in the masticator space found infranotch tumours fare about as well as T4a, while supranotch spread does far worse (5-year survival 55.3% vs 14.3% in one series). Complications averaged 37.9%; one series needed tracheotomy in 92% and gastrostomy in 84%. Offer it in high-volume centres and plan airway and feeding early.

cards.head: Bone flaps halve plate problems versus soft flap plus plate
cards.rib: Keep plate-and-soft-flap for patients unfit for a bone flap.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 2,379 patients with segmental jaw defects and at least a year of follow-up compared soft-tissue flaps over a reconstruction plate with vascularised bone flaps. Plate exposure was 20% vs 10%, plate fracture 5% vs 1%, and repeat surgery 32% vs 14%. When the patient can tolerate it, rebuild segmental mandible defects with bone rather than a bridging plate.

cards.head: Nerve-joined tongue flaps feel more; function gain unproven
cards.rib: Coapt the lingual nerve when practical; counsel on modest gains.
cards.take: A systematic review of 14 studies (271 tongue reconstructions, mostly radial forearm and ALT flaps) asked whether joining a sensory nerve to the flap helps. All 7 head-to-head studies found better sensation in reinnervated flaps, and 4 of 5 found radiotherapy did not spoil recovery. Proof that this improves speech or swallowing is still weak. Join the nerve when easy, but don't promise function.

cards.ev: Cohort · J Cancer Res Clin Oncol 2026

fig.from: Ketschau, J Cancer Res Clin Oncol 2026
fig.title: Occult nodes by CT-to-surgery gap

cards.head: Usual waits from CT to surgery didn't raise hidden nodes
cards.rib: Short waits are fine; don't let staging-to-surgery pass 30 days.
cards.take: A Munich cohort of 329 node-negative oral cancers checked the gap between staging CT and surgery (median 9 days). Hidden neck nodes turned up in 16.1%. The link with waiting time vanished after adjustment; only the 13 patients who waited over 30 days had a high node rate (7 of 13). Routine scheduling gaps look safe, but keep the wait under a month.

cards.ev: Phase II/III RCT · J Clin Oncol 2022
cards.head: Weekly cisplatin 40 is as good as 3-weekly after surgery
cards.rib: Postop CRT: weekly cisplatin 40 is a fair swap for 3-weekly 100.
cards.take: In JCOG1008, 261 high-risk patients having radiotherapy after head and neck surgery were randomised to cisplatin 40 mg/m² weekly or 100 mg/m² every 3 weeks. Weekly dosing proved non-inferior: 3-year survival 71.6% vs 59.1% (HR 0.69). Severe neutropenia, infection and kidney harm were less common with weekly dosing, though hearing loss was more frequent. Weekly 40 mg/m² is a sound postoperative choice.

cards.ev: Landmark case series · Plast Reconstr Surg 1986
cards.head: 1986: scapula flap rebuilt jaws and palates with no failures
cards.rib: Think scapula when skin and bone must sit apart in 3D
cards.take: Swartz and colleagues injected 8 cadavers, then used the lateral scapular border flap in 26 patients with jaw or maxillectomy defects. Up to 14 cm of straight bone came on the circumflex scapular vessels, the thin blade suited palate and orbital floor, and skin panels moved independently of the bone. No flaps failed and donor problems were minimal. Consider it for complex 3D midface repair.

cards.head: Quit tobacco 10 years: cheek cancer odds fall up to 61%
cards.rib: Tell chewers it is never too late: risk drops within 5 years
cards.take: Tata Memorial and Oxford researchers compared 2,320 Indians with buccal mucosa cancer against 2,302 controls. People who quit smoking 10 or more years earlier had 61% lower odds than current smokers (OR 0.39); ex-chewers had 42% lower odds (OR 0.58). Risk fell fastest after about 5 years. Chewing products containing areca nut raised odds 1.86-fold. Quitting pays at any stage.

cards.ev: Landmark case series · Plast Reconstr Surg 1979
cards.head: 1979: the pec major flap that reshaped head and neck repair
cards.rib: Every free-flap surgeon should still be able to raise a pec major
cards.take: In 1979 Ariyan described a flap of chest skin carried on a narrow strip of pectoralis major muscle with its axial vessels. It closed large head and neck defects in all 4 of his first patients and promised more versatility than the deltopectoral flap then in use. Decades later it is still the go-to backup when a free flap is not possible or has failed.

cards.head: Orbit floor rebuilds: soft tissue alone droops the eyelid
cards.rib: Keep the eye? Give the orbital floor bone or mesh, not just bulk
cards.take: After Brown class III maxillectomy, 20 studies compared ways to rebuild the orbital floor. Ectropion (lower lid turning out) was common overall at 42.6%, worst with soft-tissue-only repairs (63%) and least with free bone flaps (14%). Enophthalmos affected 9.6% and double vision 6.6%. When the orbital floor goes but the eye stays, give it rigid support with a bony flap or an alloplastic implant.

fig.title: Mean fibula height loss over 54 months

cards.head: Fibula bone keeps its height for years in the new jaw
cards.rib: Bone loss is small, so plan implants in fibula with confidence
cards.take: Memorial Sloan Kettering measured fibula height on panoramic X-rays in 27 jaw reconstructions, followed for a mean of 54 months. Height fell only 4% at the chin, 7% in the body and 5% in the ramus, and 93% of osteotomies united. Radiotherapy, age, implants and follow-up length shifted height by 10% or less. The vascularised fibula keeps enough bone for later dental implants.

cards.head: Leeches have the best evidence for rescuing congested flaps
cards.rib: Re-explore a congested flap first; leeches are the backup
cards.take: A review of 72 articles found 17 ways to manage a flap with venous congestion: 7 before or during surgery and 10 afterwards. Most evidence was weak. Leeches stood out, with enough patients and follow-up to support their use. Heparin scarification, catheter bleeding, negative pressure and hyperbaric oxygen lacked solid proof. Fix a correctable vein problem first; leeches are the best-supported backup.

fig.from: de Koning, in Spence OTO Open 2024
fig.title: Clear margin of 5 mm or more

cards.head: Ultrasound in theatre tracks tongue tumour depth closely
cards.rib: Use an intraoral probe to plan the deep margin in tongue cancer
cards.take: Twelve studies (232 patients) tested ultrasound during tongue cancer surgery. Its tumour thickness matched final pathology closely (pooled correlation 0.92, mean gap under 0.7 mm). In the largest comparison, clear margins of 5 mm or more rose from 16% to 55% and positive margins fell from 15% to 5%. Data are small and retrospective, but it is a cheap deep-cut guide.

lines: ALT donor wound breakdown vs RFF

cards.head: ALT donor sites cause fewer wound and limb problems
cards.rib: If both flaps fit the defect, the thigh spares donor function
cards.take: Eighteen cohort studies (1,018 patients) compared donor sites of the anterolateral thigh (535) and radial forearm (483) flaps. The thigh had far fewer wound breakdowns (OR 0.2) and much less loss of strength (OR 0.18) or movement (OR 0.19). Numbness was similar overall but lower with ALT in tongue repairs. Infection, seroma and appearance did not differ. When both fit, the thigh is kinder.

cards.head: Iliac crest and fibula rebuild the jaw equally well
cards.rib: Match the bone to the defect: height for iliac, length for fibula.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 24 studies found no difference in total flap loss between iliac crest and fibula flaps for the mandible. Iliac flaps had more recipient-site wound breakdown; fibula legs had slightly more donor problems, and dental implants were lost more in fibula (5.3% vs 1.7%). Practical point: iliac suits angle-body defects needing height; fibula suits long, subtotal defects.

cards.head: Gene risk brings cancer 10 years early in tobacco chewers
cards.rib: Quitting tobacco matters most; gene scores may sharpen screening.
cards.take: Tata Memorial's genome study of 2,160 Indian buccal cancer patients and 2,325 controls found risk genes near TERT and the HLA immune region, plus new spots near NOTCH1 in a multi-country analysis. Chewers with a high combined gene-risk score developed cancer about 10 years earlier. Practical point: tobacco remains the main cause; gene scores may later help target screening.

cards.head: Triple oral metronomic beat second-line usual care
cards.rib: Offer oral triple metronomic when second-line IO is out of reach.
cards.take: In a 16-centre Indian phase 3 trial of 114 patients whose head and neck cancer had failed or could not take platinum, daily oral methotrexate, celecoxib and erlotinib lived longer than physician's choice therapy: median 181 vs 123 days (HR 0.58). Toxicity was lower too. Practical point: a cheap, home-based oral regimen is a valid second-line option when immunotherapy is unaffordable.

lines: of bony flaps got ORN after RT
a third of those lost the flap

cards.head: Bone flaps get ORN too: 1 in 5 after radiotherapy
cards.rib: Stop smoking and treat plate exposure early in irradiated flaps.
cards.take: Of 112 patients given postoperative radiotherapy after a bony free flap jaw rebuild, 21 (19%) developed osteoradionecrosis in the flap, on average 19 months later; a third of them lost the whole flap. Smoking (OR 5.8) and earlier plate exposure (OR 5.6) were the strong predictors. Practical point: push smoking cessation, fix plate exposure early and watch irradiated bone flaps long term.

fig.from: Ooms et al, J Clin Med 2024
fig.title: Flap success by recipient artery

cards.head: Any healthy neck recipient vessel feeds the flap equally
cards.rib: Choose recipient vessels for quality and reach, not by name.
cards.take: In 338 forearm, thigh and fibula flaps, the choice of artery (external carotid, facial, lingual or superior thyroid) or vein (internal jugular, its branches or external jugular) made no difference to measured flap blood flow or oxygen, or to flap success (96 to 100%). Practical point: pick the recipient vessel that is healthy, well matched and lies without tension.

cards.head: Pre-op pembrolizumab: fewer positive margins in KEYNOTE-689
cards.rib: Hypothesis-generating subgroup data; surgery stays on track.
cards.take: An exploratory KEYNOTE-689 analysis (ASCO 2026 poster) of 714 resectable patients: adding pembrolizumab before and after surgery cut positive margins (19.9% vs 29.9%) and extranodal spread (25.5% vs 36.4%) with similar numbers reaching surgery. Event-free survival benefit held whether margins were clear or not. Practical point: neoadjuvant immunotherapy does not compromise resection and may ease it.

cards.head: Implant teeth give the best mouth comfort after jaw flaps
cards.rib: Plan dental implants at the time of bony flap reconstruction.
cards.take: Of 113 Salzburg patients with bony free-flap jaw rebuilds, only 27% got implant-supported teeth, 24% got plain dentures and nearly half got nothing. Implants lost 18% (82% survived). Oral-health burden scores (lower is better) were 7 with implant teeth, 30.5 with none and 54 with conventional dentures. Practical point: plan implants with the reconstruction; loose dentures on a flap help little.

cards.ev: Systematic review · Eur J Surg Oncol 2017
cards.head: Selective neck dissection spares the shoulder the most
cards.rib: Choose the smallest safe dissection and refer early to physio.
cards.take: A systematic review of 75 studies tracked shoulder and neck problems after neck dissection. Shoulder pain was reported in 10–100% after radical, 0–100% after modified radical and 9–25% after selective dissection. Reduced shoulder movement affected 5–20% and reduced neck movement 1–13%. Saving the accessory nerve lowers but does not remove the risk. Warn patients and start shoulder physiotherapy early.

cards.head: Bone gaps over 1 mm stop jaw flap segments uniting
cards.rib: Plan cuts so bone ends touch; check union on follow-up scans.
cards.take: CT review of 104 bony free flaps for the jaw and maxilla found 37% of bone contacts only partly united or not united. Flap meeting native jaw united less often than flap-to-flap joins (53% vs 65%). A gap of 1 mm or more rarely went on to full union, and poor union meant more wound problems (40% vs 19%). Cut and fit osteotomies flush.

fig.title: Local recurrence by DNA margin status

cards.head: Clear margins can still hide tumour DNA and predict relapse
cards.rib: Clear on the slide is not always clear; respect field change.
cards.take: In a 1995 landmark study, 25 head and neck cancers carrying a p53 mutation and with microscopically clear margins were retested with a DNA test. The tumour's mutation turned up in at least one margin in 13 patients. Five of those 13 (38%) recurred locally, versus none of the 12 with DNA-clear margins. The test also found cancer cells in 21% of 'negative' nodes.

cards.head: Flap after hemiglossectomy eased speech and swallowing
cards.rib: Small single-centre study: weigh longer surgery against function.
cards.take: A Thai study of 70 patients after partial to hemi-glossectomy compared flap reconstruction with primary closure 6–12 months later. Flap patients reported fewer symptoms overall (HN35 score 40.9 vs 44.7) and better swallowing and speech, even after adjusting for stage and adjuvant therapy. The cost was longer surgery and more wound problems (14.3% vs 0%). Consider flaps for intermediate tongue defects.

cards.head: Under 1 in 100 Indian women aged 30–49 had oral screening
cards.rib: Examine the mouth of every tobacco user at every clinic visit.
cards.take: An analysis of India's NFHS-5 survey (2019–21) covering 348,882 women aged 30–49 found only 0.87% had ever been screened for oral cancer. Coverage was lower in rural areas (0.77% vs 1.08% urban), among the poorest (0.37%) and among rural tobacco users (0.39%), the very group at highest risk. Southern India led at 2.31%. Take screening to tobacco users and villages.

cards.head: Durvalumab around chemoradiation did not help throat cancer
cards.rib: Keep cisplatin chemoradiation as standard for oropharynx cancer.
cards.take: The UK CompARE phase III trial randomised 594 people with intermediate- or high-risk oropharyngeal cancer to cisplatin chemoradiation alone or with durvalumab before and for 6 months after. Three-year survival was 84% versus 82% (HR 0.97). A non-significant trend favoured durvalumab in high-risk HPV-negative patients (65% vs 52%). Cisplatin chemoradiation stays standard. Meeting abstract, ESMO 2025.

cards.head: Vasopressors during free flap surgery do not harm flaps
cards.rib: Use vasopressors for hypotension; avoid fluid overload instead.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 14 studies covering 8,653 free flaps compared patients given vasopressors around surgery with those not given them. Total flap failure was not higher; it was slightly lower with vasopressors (odds ratio 0.71). In head and neck flaps, pedicle clots were less frequent (OR 0.58). Only breast flaps showed more complications. Treat low blood pressure instead of flooding with fluid.

cards.ev: Systematic review · Br J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2021
cards.head: Lip-split jaw access is safe: about 5% complications each
cards.rib: When access is tight, a mandibulotomy is still a safe choice.
cards.take: A registered review of 54 studies and 3,872 patients found no deaths linked to lip-split mandibulotomy. Bone death (osteoradionecrosis) occurred in a median 5.4%, fistula in 5.7%, poor bone healing in 4.9%, and infection or plate exposure in about 5%. Swallowing and quality of life were not clearly worse. Keep this access route for hard-to-reach back-of-mouth tumours.

fig.title: Minutes from alarm to re-explore decision

cards.head: Smartphone flap photos speed the call to re-explore
cards.rib: Have nurses send flap photos so seniors can decide at once.
cards.take: In 103 free flaps at Chang Gung, surgeons judging flaps from smartphone photos were right 94.2% of the time, close to 98.7% for bedside checks. The real gain was speed: the decision to return to theatre came in about 8 minutes with photos versus 180 minutes when the surgeon had to come and see. Use photos to shorten the alarm-to-action gap.

cards.head: Periorbita breached? The eye can often still be saved
cards.rib: Resect the periorbita; exenterate only for deeper orbital spread.
cards.take: In 32 sinonasal cancers that reached the eye's lining, Prague surgeons kept the eye in 18 and removed it in 14 with deeper spread. Five-year survival was 44% with the eye kept versus 34% with removal, not a significant gap. After radiotherapy, 61% kept unchanged vision, though 28% lost useful sight. Small study, but periorbital spread alone need not mean exenteration.

cards.head: Crossing to the other side of the neck saves flaps
cards.rib: Depleted neck side? Plan a long pedicle to the other side.
cards.take: When one side of the neck had no usable vessels, a German centre joined the flap to vessels on the opposite side in 32 of 318 free flaps (10%). Superior thyroid artery and facial vein were the usual partners; 30 were long-pedicle forearm flaps. Problems hit 4 patients (12.5%), yet no flap was lost. A long-pedicle flap plus contralateral vessels is a dependable plan.

cards.head: Scapula spares the leg and offers a second-chance flap
cards.rib: For maxilla or frail patients, consider scapula over fibula.
cards.take: Comparing 114 fibula and 42 scapula flaps over 24 years, flap trouble rates were similar. Fibula suited the lower jaw and scapula the upper jaw. Donor-site problems hit 7.9% of fibula cases and none of the scapula cases, and hospital stay was shorter with scapula. A failed scapula could be replaced from the other shoulder; a failed fibula could not.

cards.head: Chemo first makes 1 in 4 'unresectable' cancers operable
cards.rib: Re-image after induction chemo; operate on those who respond.
cards.take: At Tata Memorial Varanasi, 119 technically unresectable head and neck cancers (87% oral) got chemotherapy before deciding on surgery. Tumours shrank partly in about 4 in 10; none vanished. Surgery became possible in 33 patients (28%). Those operated lived a median 18 months versus 9 months without surgery. Reassess after chemo, because a resectable minority does far better.

cards.ev: Cohort · Int J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2008
cards.head: Only 1 in 4 fibula jaw patients get their teeth back
cards.rib: Plan implants at the first visit or most patients never get them.
cards.take: Of 70 patients whose jaw was rebuilt with a fibula flap in Rotterdam, 24 received implants and only 18 (about 26%) finished full dental rehabilitation. The main reason was not technique but the short survival of many oral cancer patients. Gains from implant-held dentures were mostly cosmetic. Plan teeth early, and pick patients most likely to benefit.

cards.head: Plate the radius and forearm bone flaps rarely fracture
cards.rib: Plate the radius at harvest and take only the bone you need.
cards.take: In 167 jaw rebuilds with the bony forearm flap (median 7 cm of radius), routine plating of the donor radius kept fractures to a single case (0.5%). The cost was elsewhere: tendon exposure in 28%, hand weakness or numbness in 9%, and jaw plate exposure in 17%. Each extra centimetre of bone raised plate-exposure odds 1.3-fold. Plate the radius; keep bone short.

cards.head: Hyperbaric oxygen did not heal established jaw ORN
cards.rib: For overt jaw ORN, skip HBO; use medical or surgical treatment.
cards.take: The ORN96 trial gave 68 patients with exposed-bone jaw osteoradionecrosis 30 hyperbaric oxygen sessions before surgery and 10 after, or a blinded placebo. It stopped early because oxygen looked worse. At one year 19% healed with oxygen versus 32% with placebo, and pain relief was no faster. For overt ORN, do not count on hyperbaric oxygen; plan medical and surgical treatment.

cards.head: TAX 324: adding docetaxel to induction PF extends survival
cards.rib: When induction is chosen, use TPF and watch for low white counts.
cards.take: TAX 324 randomised 501 patients with unresectable or organ-preservation stage III-IV head and neck cancer to induction cisplatin-5FU with or without docetaxel (TPF), then carboplatin chemoradiation. TPF lowered the risk of death by 30%: 3-year survival 62% versus 48%, median 71 versus 30 months. Expect more neutropenia. If you use induction, TPF is the regimen to choose.

lines: had a clear margin under 5 mm

cards.head: Buccal cancer: deep margin falls short; RT beats re-cutting
cards.rib: Guard the deep margin; if close, favour postop RT over a recut.
cards.take: In 97 Dutch patients with buccal mucosa cancer, 23% recurred locally. Nine in ten had a tumour-free margin under 5 mm, and the deep margin was the one most often short. Larger pT3 tumours, past smoking, margin status and postoperative (chemo)radiation predicted local control. Going back to re-resect a close margin did not improve control; adjuvant radiotherapy may be the better fix.

cards.head: Postop RT: 57.6 Gy to the bed, 63 Gy where nodes burst
cards.rib: Ask for at least 57.6 Gy, boost ENE necks to 63 Gy, start early.
cards.take: This MD Anderson trial randomised postoperative patients to radiotherapy doses from 52.2 to 68.4 Gy (1.8 Gy a day). Doses of 54 Gy or less let more cancers return at the primary than 57.6 Gy or more. Going higher helped only necks with extranodal spread, which did better at 63 Gy. Above 63 Gy, side-effects rose without gain. Start radiotherapy promptly after surgery.

cards.head: Head and neck cancers often break skin-maturing genes
cards.rib: Blocked cell maturation is a core driver, beyond TP53 and tobacco.
cards.take: Sequencing the protein-coding genes of 74 head and neck cancers against normal tissue showed most carried the fingerprint of tobacco damage, and HPV could be read straight from tumour DNA. Beyond known genes such as TP53, CDKN2A and PIK3CA, at least 30% had faults in genes that make squamous cells mature, like NOTCH1, IRF6 and TP63. Faulty maturation is a key driver.

cards.head: Shaped ALT flaps rebuild lateral skull base defects
cards.rib: Chimeric or folded ALT designs suit big composite skull base gaps.
cards.take: Surgeons in China rebuilt lateral skull base defects after advanced or recurrent oral cancer surgery in 37 patients with thigh flaps, using chimeric, double, folded or combined designs for 26 through-and-through holes and muscle or fat to fill dead space. 38 of 39 flaps survived fully, one partly. Salivary leak hit 3 patients. One thigh flap, tailored, can close complex composite defects.

cards.ev: Cohort · J Oral Biol Craniofac Res 2022
cards.head: Pec major flap still rivals free flaps on complications
cards.rib: Where microsurgery or funds are short, pec major is a safe choice.
cards.take: An Indian centre reviewed five years of oral cancer reconstruction. Of 90 pectoralis major flaps, about half were chosen because microsurgery was unavailable and 43% because of cost. Complications were similar: 30% with pec major versus 28% with free flaps. Total loss was rare (one pec, two free flaps), though 13% of pec skin paddles had edge necrosis. The pec flap remains a dependable workhorse.

cards.head: De-ESCALaTE: cisplatin beats cetuximab in low-risk HPV
cards.rib: Cetuximab is not a safe swap; give cisplatin when patients can.
cards.take: De-ESCALaTE randomised 334 patients with low-risk HPV-positive throat cancer to radiotherapy with cisplatin or cetuximab. Cetuximab was no gentler: severe side-effects averaged 4.8 per patient in both arms. It was worse at curing: 2-year survival 89.4% versus 97.5%, and recurrence 16.1% versus 6.0%. If the patient can take cisplatin, keep it as the radiation partner.

cards.head: Venous coupler matches hand-sewn joins on flap survival
cards.rib: Coupler or sutures both work for veins; pick what you do best.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of free flaps from 1990–2018 compared hand-sewn venous anastomosis, the mechanical coupler and the Doppler-equipped coupler. Overall flap failure was 1.9% and venous thrombosis 3.5%. Coupler rates (failure 1.0%, thrombosis 2.2%) were numerically lower than hand-sewn (2.6%, 3.6%) but not significantly different; the Doppler coupler had 11.1% thrombosis. Choose by vessel size and your own experience.

cards.head: Toluidine blue helps but cannot screen mouths on its own
cards.rib: Dye uptake guides the biopsy site; histology still decides.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 29 studies (1,921 people) tested toluidine blue dye for oral cancer and precancer. Pooled sensitivity was 73% and specificity 69%. It beat clinical examination alone and caught severe dysplasia best, but chemiluminescence was more sensitive. Use the dye as an add-on to guide where to biopsy, never as a stand-alone screening test.

cards.head: Levels IV–V are rarely involved; skip spread under 9%
cards.rib: cN0 non-tongue: levels I–III suffice; extend for tongue primaries.
cards.take: A systematic review of 32 studies examined how often oral cavity cancer spreads to the lower neck. Skip metastasis to level IV or V, bypassing levels I–III, reached at most 8.5%, and only 1.8% in clinically node-negative necks. The authors support levels I–III for elective dissection, adding lower levels for tongue cancer. Evidence is retrospective and heterogeneous.

cards.head: Free flaps in over-75s: 94% succeed with careful selection
cards.rib: Do a geriatric assessment and keep anaesthesia time short.
cards.take: Three Italian centres reviewed 84 patients aged 75 or older (12 over 85) given free flaps for advanced oral cancer. Flap success was 94.1%, but 61.9% had at least one complication; major surgical complications hit 20.2%. Higher ASA score, diabetes and longer anaesthesia drove complications. Age alone should not bar a free flap; assess fitness, control sugar, operate efficiently.

cards.head: ERAS pathways cut free flap stays by about 4 days
cards.rib: Use one written ERAS pathway for every free flap patient.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 18 studies (2,630 patients) compared enhanced recovery (ERAS) pathways with usual care after head and neck free flap surgery. ERAS shortened hospital stay by 4.4 days, lowered readmission (OR 0.64) and wound complications (RR 0.41), without more reoperations or deaths. Components varied between centres. Adopt a written, team-wide pathway rather than ad hoc care.

cards.ev: Phase II trial · Clin Cancer Res 2020
cards.head: One pre-op pembrolizumab dose: response in 44%, no delays
cards.rib: Pre-op immunotherapy did not delay surgery or raise risks.
cards.take: In a phase II trial, 36 patients with resectable HPV-unrelated head and neck cancer had one pembrolizumab dose 2–3 weeks before surgery. There were no grade 3–4 serious events or surgical delays. 44% showed some tumour-bed response, 22% a major one, none complete. High-risk patients relapsed at one year in 16.7% (historical 35%). A window dose is safe; KEYNOTE-689 took it to phase III.

cards.head: Specimen-driven frozen sections beat defect-driven checks
cards.rib: Assess margins on the specimen, with the surgeon orienting it.
cards.take: A review of 18 studies compared ways of checking oral cancer margins during surgery. For soft tissue, sampling the resected specimen detected inadequate margins more often than sampling the wound bed (sensitivity 68.4% vs 47.6%; specificity 96.7% vs 84.4%). For bone, specimen-driven checks reached 81.8% sensitivity. Few defect-driven studies exist. Ink and examine the specimen itself rather than shaving the defect.

cards.head: Under-40 oral cancer fares no worse than in older adults
cards.rib: Treat young tongue cancer by stage and pathology, not by age.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 22 studies (23,382 patients) compared oral cavity cancer in adults aged 40 or under with older patients after curative treatment. Nine in ten young patients had tongue primaries, mostly T1–T2. Pooled overall survival was the same (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.66–1.41). Young age alone is not a reason to escalate surgery or add adjuvant therapy.

fig.title: Neck relapse in cN0 sinonasal cancer

cards.head: Elective neck treatment cuts sinonasal neck relapse by 62%
cards.rib: Plan neck treatment with the maxillectomy, not after relapse.
cards.take: This review pooled 26 retrospective series of node-negative sinonasal cancers (1,178 patients, most arising in the maxillary sinus). Neck relapse was 5.9% after elective neck dissection or irradiation versus 15% with observation, an odds ratio of 0.38. Any survival gain remains uncertain. Consider treating the node-negative neck, especially in maxillary sinus squamous cancer, when planning maxillectomy.

cards.head: Colour Doppler finds ALT perforators as well as CT angiogram
cards.rib: Use colour Doppler mapping where CT angiography is costly or slow.
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 23 studies checked preoperative imaging against what surgeons found at ALT harvest. Colour Doppler ultrasound detected 95.3% of perforators versus 90.4% for CT angiography, with similar false positives (2.8% vs 2.4%). Both predicted the perforator course through or around muscle in about 96%. Colour Doppler is a radiation-free, cheaper option when an experienced sonologist is available.

cards.head: Manipur extends one-year ban on gutkha and chewing tobacco
cards.rib: Use the ban to reinforce quit advice for chewers in clinic.
cards.take: Manipur has extended its ban on making, storing, transporting and selling gutkha and pan masala containing tobacco or nicotine, plus chewing tobacco such as khaini and flavoured tobacco. The state food safety notification dated 27 October 2026 runs for one year. The report gives no penalty or enforcement figures. Smokeless tobacco is a leading cause of oral cancer, so quitting advice remains central.

cards.head: Forearm flaps with two veins fail three times less often
cards.rib: Add a second vein when a suitable recipient is available.
cards.take: Utrecht tracked consecutive forearm free flaps for 25 years (1998-2023). Flaps drained by a single vein needed vascular re-exploration more often (8.3% vs 2.8%) and failed more often (6.7% vs 2.0%) than flaps with two venous anastomoses. A single vein independently predicted both revision and failure. When a second suitable vein is available, add the second venous anastomosis.

cards.head: Vein-grafted free flaps fail in about 1 in 8
cards.rib: Look for a graft-free recipient first; counsel on higher risk.
cards.take: This review pooled 11 studies of 789 head and neck free flaps that needed vein grafts, usually because nearby recipient vessels were missing. Pooled flap failure was 12.3%, well above typical free flap loss, though results varied widely between studies. Vein grafts remain a reliable bridge when needed, but counsel patients about the higher risk and look first for recipients that avoid grafting.

cards.head: Nivolumab biosimilars cut cost to about Rs 30,000 a cycle
cards.rib: Revisit immunotherapy for patients who once could not afford it.
cards.take: Biosimilar nivolumab has cut the cost of one cycle in India from over Rs 1 lakh to about Rs 30,000 in some cases; a Mumbai oncologist reports immunotherapy prescriptions up over 50% in six months. A 2022 Tata Memorial study found only 2.8% of eligible patients received immunotherapy. More versions may bring prices near Rs 10,000. Press report, not trial data.

cards.head: Genetically mixed tumours carry double the death risk
cards.rib: A promising risk marker, but not yet one to change treatment.
cards.take: Using gene sequencing from 305 TCGA head and neck cancers, researchers scored how varied the cancer cells were within each tumour (the MATH score). Highly mixed tumours had 2.2 times the risk of death, and this held after allowing for age, HPV, grade, TP53 and nodal stage, including in oral cavity cancers. It is not yet a routine test; prospective validation is still needed.

cards.head: Buccal cancer 13 mm or more from skin: cheek skin can stay
cards.rib: Measure tumour-to-skin distance on imaging before removing skin.
cards.take: In 331 buccal mucosa cancers from Chang Gung, Taiwan, cheek skin was kept when imaging showed tumour at least 13 mm from the skin (1 cm margin plus 3 mm of skin). Five-year local control was similar whether skin was removed or kept: 94% vs 91% after surgery alone and 82% vs 86% with adjuvant therapy. Measure tumour-to-skin distance on imaging before planning skin excision.

cards.head: Pec major problems are common but rarely need a new flap
cards.rib: Correct albumin and nutrition first; expect minor wound issues.
cards.take: Memorial Sloan Kettering reviewed 211 pectoralis major myocutaneous flaps. Flap-related problems such as partial necrosis, wound breakdown, fistula or infection affected 63%, doubling median hospital stay (33 vs 16 days). Yet only 26% of those needed another operation and just 2 patients needed a second flap. Older age, female sex, obesity, albumin below 4 g/dL and big glossectomy repairs raised risk.

cards.head: Jaw ORN over 3× likelier when >14% of jaw gets 60 Gy
cards.rib: Ask your radiation team for jaw V60 and keep it under 14%.
cards.take: This Japanese review of 616 patients given curative or postoperative radiotherapy found jaw osteoradionecrosis in 46 (7.5%), appearing a median 27 months after treatment. Two factors stood out independently: more than 14% of the jaw receiving 60 Gy, and an oral or oropharyngeal primary. Three-year ORN was 8.6% versus 2.5%. Ask planners to keep jaw V60 low and follow these patients for years.

cards.head: TPEx matched EXTREME survival with less severe toxicity
cards.rib: Where immunotherapy is unaffordable, TPEx is a gentler base.
cards.take: In 541 patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer, GORTEC's TPExtreme compared docetaxel-cisplatin-cetuximab (TPEx) with the EXTREME regimen as first-line treatment. Median survival was similar, 14.5 vs 13.4 months, but grade 4 or worse toxicity fell from 52% to 36%, and more patients finished planned cycles. When cetuximab-chemo is chosen, TPEx is a kinder, shorter option.

cards.head: Oral margins shrink by a third to a half after removal
cards.rib: Aim for a 1 cm cut in vivo to report a clear 5 mm on slides.
cards.take: Measuring margins in the mouth before cutting and again under the microscope, Johnson and colleagues found they shrank by about 31% on tongue surface mucosa, 35% in deep tongue muscle and 47% in cheek and lip mucosa, mostly right after excision. A 5 mm pathology margin may have been about 7 to 9 mm in the patient. Plan a 1 cm clinical cut.

cards.head: Radiation raises implant failure risk by about 60%
cards.rib: Implants remain worthwhile after RT; counsel on higher failure.
cards.take: This update of 2021–2024 studies (7 in the meta-analysis) found implant survival of 85.6% in irradiated head and neck cancer patients versus 90.0% without radiation. Radiation raised failure risk 1.6-fold, chemoradiation about 2-fold, and implants in grafted or flap bone failed twice as often as in native bone. Implants still work, but plan longer follow-up and careful hygiene.

cards.head: Five flap monitoring tools beat bedside checks alone
cards.rib: Add a monitoring aid to clinical checks; phone photos count too.
cards.take: Reviewing 184 publications on free flap monitoring, Chae and colleagues found comparative evidence of better flap salvage for five tools: implantable Doppler, near-infrared spectroscopy, laser Doppler flowmetry, quantitative fluorimetry and smartphone photography. Implantable Doppler had the most supporting studies. Clinical checks stay the base; add a device, or even phone photos, where resources allow.

cards.head: Worst pattern of invasion 5 flags hidden nodes
cards.rib: Ask for WPOI on reports; WPOI-5 tips early cases toward the neck.
cards.take: A 2026 review of worst pattern of invasion (WPOI) in oral cancer gathers the evidence: aggressive patterns (WPOI 4–5) roughly double the risk of death (pooled hazard ratio 2.17), and WPOI-5 tumours hid neck nodes in 62.5% versus 34.8% for lower grades. Scoring is not yet standardised. Ask pathologists to report WPOI, and weigh it when deciding neck treatment.

cards.head: p16-positive but HPV-negative throat cancer fares worse
cards.rib: Check HPV DNA or RNA after a positive p16 before de-escalating.
cards.take: Pooling 7,654 oropharyngeal cancers from 13 cohorts, 11% of p16-positive tumours were HPV-negative, and 7.5% of p16-negative ones were HPV-positive. These mismatched cases had 5-year survival of only about 54%, versus 81% when both tests were positive. A p16 stain alone can misjudge prognosis; confirm HPV directly before de-escalating treatment or counselling.

cards.head: 1 in 10 legs has a variant artery pattern
cards.rib: Image the legs of smokers and arteriopaths before fibula harvest.
cards.take: Dissecting 162 legs, this anatomical study found the usual three-vessel pattern in 90.7%; 6.2% had a weak or absent posterior tibial artery, making the peroneal vital to the foot. Atherosclerosis makes such variants commoner in living patients. If routine leg CT angiography is not possible, image those with vascular risk factors and check foot pulses before fibula harvest.

cards.head: Pre-surgery nivolumab shrank oral cancers without delay
cards.rib: Pre-op immunotherapy is safe to test; surgery stays standard.
cards.take: In a window trial, 29 untreated oral cavity cancers received nivolumab alone or with ipilimumab for a few weeks before surgery. About half shrank on scans (50% and 53%), pathological downstaging was seen in 53% and 69%, and no operation was delayed. Major pathological responses were few (1 of 14 vs 3 of 15). Promising, but keep it within trials for now.

fig.title: Health worker visual exam vs doctors

cards.head: Trained health workers spot mouth precancer like doctors
cards.rib: Train frontline workers to screen high-risk mouths routinely.
cards.take: Within the Kerala oral screening trial, mouth examinations by 14 trained health workers were checked against three doctors in 2,069 people. Workers picked up 94% of true lesions and correctly cleared 99% of normal mouths. Agreement with doctors on lesion type was almost perfect (kappa 0.85), and accuracy grew with experience. Practical point: trained frontline workers can reliably run visual oral screening.

cards.head: cT4b buccal cancer: upfront surgery gives 59% 5-yr survival
cards.rib: CT overcalls masticator spread; resect when margins can be clear.
cards.take: Tata Medical Center, Kolkata, operated upfront on 104 buccal cancers staged cT4b for masticator space spread. Pathology confirmed masticator involvement in only 36; CT was sensitive (92%) but often overcalled. Margins were clear in 76%. Five-year overall survival was 58.6%. Involved margins and more than one positive node predicted poor outcome. Practical point: do not call cT4b buccal cancer inoperable; aim for clear margins.

cards.head: Lateral buccal-gum cancer: neck RT can stay one-sided
cards.rib: Spare the opposite neck when the tumour sits well off the midline.
cards.take: A Taiwanese team followed 149 patients with well-lateralised buccal, gum or retromolar cancers, mostly T3-T4, for a median 5.2 years. Five-year opposite-neck failure as first relapse was only 3.6%, never isolated, and none occurred in irradiated patients. Excluded were tumours within 1 cm of midline, tongue or floor of mouth, level Ia nodes, bilateral nodes and ENE. Practical point: unilateral PORT suits such patients.

fig.title: High vs low node ratio, node-positive OSCC

cards.head: High lymph node ratio flags worse survival in oral cancer
cards.rib: Report node ratio with node yield to sharpen adjuvant decisions.
cards.take: This 2022 meta-analysis pooled 32 studies with almost 21,000 oral cancer patients. Lymph node ratio is positive nodes divided by all nodes removed. Among node-positive patients, a high ratio raised the risk of death by about 68% and of cancer death by 94%. Cut-offs ranged from 0.012 to 0.2. Practical point: report node yield and ratio, and weigh a high ratio when planning adjuvant therapy.

cards.head: Out of bed within 2 days: fewer complications after flaps
cards.rib: Early movement does not harm flaps; delay brings chest infections.
cards.take: In 445 Calgary enhanced-recovery patients after head and neck free-flap surgery, 77% were mobilised by day 2. Those mobilised later had more pneumonia (18% vs 5%), longer stays (median 14 vs 10 days) and higher odds of major complications (OR 2.61). Flap loss stayed about 1% either way. Tracheostomy and ICU stay delayed mobilisation. Practical point: get flap patients out of bed within 48 hours.

cards.head: Pedicle redo and long ischaemia predict free flap loss
cards.rib: Get the first anastomosis right and keep ischaemia time short.
cards.take: Among 892 head and neck free flaps at one US centre over ten years, 4.8% failed. Flaps whose pedicle needed revision during the first operation had nearly 10-fold higher odds of failure. Each extra 5 minutes of ischaemia raised failure odds by about 6%, and postoperative alcohol withdrawal by about 3.7-fold. Practical point: keep ischaemia short and watch revised flaps and heavy drinkers closely.

cards.head: India revises prices of 543 cancer drug brands from Nov 9
cards.rib: Many cancer drugs get cheaper; immunotherapy prices stay high.
cards.take: India's drug price regulator NPPA has notified revised retail prices for 543 anti-cancer brands, effective 9 November 2026, after capping trade margins on 137 non-scheduled cancer medicines. Hindi press reports say 397 brands got cheaper, 217 by more than half, while immunotherapies such as pembrolizumab (Keytruda) stayed unchanged. Practical point: recheck patients' drug cost estimates after 9 November.

cards.head: Plate plus soft flap for jaw gaps: plate exposed in 46%
cards.rib: Bridging plates fail often; rebuild segmental gaps with bone.
cards.take: This 2003 series followed 65 men whose jaw defects were bridged by a titanium plate covered with a soft-tissue free flap, mostly ALT. Complications hit 69%; plate exposure alone, 46%. Nearly a third (31%) later needed a fibula flap, at about 11.5 months, for exposure, contour loss, contracture or trismus. Practical point: rebuild segmental mandible defects with vascularised bone when the patient can tolerate it.

cards.head: Scapula donor site: 1 in 10 complications, mild arm loss
cards.rib: Offer early shoulder physio to every scapula flap patient.
cards.take: Across 24 studies of 660 head and neck reconstructions using scapular bone, the pooled donor-site complication rate was 10.7%. Shoulder and arm function was only mildly affected, with a mean DASH disability score of 14.4 out of 100. The scapula is a reasonable bone choice when leg vessels or walking are a concern, but warn patients and start shoulder physiotherapy early.

cards.head: Vessel-depleted neck is often a myth: 96% of flaps lived
cards.rib: Before settling for a pedicled flap, check the other neck too.
cards.take: In 52 patients who needed three or more major flaps, 186 flaps were done (178 free). Overall flap survival was 96.1%, with only seven failures, even though nearly half followed radiotherapy. One in five free flaps used vessels from the opposite neck, and prior radiation raised that need about fourfold. Usable recipient vessels can usually still be found; explore before giving up on free tissue.

cards.head: Selpercatinib keeps RET medullary thyroid cancer in check
cards.rib: Order RET testing early in advanced medullary thyroid cancer.
cards.take: Updated phase III LIBRETTO-531 results at ESMO 2026 compared first-line selpercatinib with cabozantinib or vandetanib in 291 people with RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer. Three-year progression-free survival was 75% versus 25%, and three-year overall survival 92% versus 75%. Severe side effects and stopping treatment were less common with selpercatinib. Test advanced medullary thyroid cancer for RET early. Meeting abstract; company-funded trial.

cards.head: T4b buccal cancer: ITF clearance gives 48% 3-year survival
cards.rib: Do not label every T4b buccal cancer inoperable; select carefully.
cards.take: Of 91 patients with cT4b buccal mucosa cancer treated with infratemporal fossa clearance, 54.9% were alive and disease-free at a median 27 months. Three-year overall survival was 48% and disease-free survival 44%. Spread into the maxillary sinus, nodal disease and no response to induction chemotherapy predicted worse survival, and high ITF disease spread more often to distant sites. Selected T4b buccal cancers merit surgery.

fig.title: Flap salvage by time to theatre

cards.head: Back to theatre within 3 hours saves five times more flaps
cards.rib: Agree a fast-track theatre plan before the first postop night.
cards.take: In 1,569 free flaps from an Australian centre, 2% developed vessel compromise and overall failure was 1.5%. Bony head and neck flaps had about 3.8 times the odds of trouble. Salvage reached 57.1% when patients returned to theatre within 3 hours of detection, but only 11.1% after longer delays. Treat a suspicious flap as an emergency and keep a theatre pathway ready.

cards.head: Bony free flaps for the maxilla succeed in 93%
cards.rib: Pick fibula or iliac crest when implant-borne teeth are the goal.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 837 patients given bony free flaps for maxillary defects found 93% flap success. About one in six (15.9%) developed a fistula. Speech was intelligible in 91% and 81% ate an unrestricted diet. Only 23.5% received dental implants: fibula 33% and iliac crest 37% versus scapula 14%. Choose the bone with dental rehabilitation in mind, and plan implants from the start.

cards.head: Zygomatic implants survive in 97% after maxillary surgery
cards.rib: Consider zygomatic anchorage early when planning maxillary rehab.
cards.take: Pooling 17 studies with 294 patients and 679 zygomatic implants, survival was 97%. Failure was 2% when implants went in at the cancer operation and 9% when placed later, a difference that was not statistically clear. Radiotherapy raised failure odds about 3.4-fold, but this too fell just short of significance. Zygomatic implants reliably anchor teeth after maxillectomy, even without bone flaps.

cards.head: Supranotch masticator spread: margins clear far less often
cards.rib: Above the notch, plan a wider compartment clearance and counsel.
cards.take: An international study of 132 oral cancers invading the masticator space compared tumours below versus above the sigmoid notch. Clear margins were achieved in 43.3% of infranotch cases but only 23.1% of supranotch ones, and positive margins were 23.9% versus 41.5%. Supranotch spread carried about 2.5 times the odds of involved margins. Plan high ITF resections carefully and counsel patients realistically.

fig.title: ICOR proposed T stage with depth (DOI)

cards.head: Depth of invasion sharpened oral cancer T staging
cards.rib: This work shaped AJCC 8th edition; insist on depth in reports.
cards.take: An 11-centre study of 3,149 surgically treated oral cancers found depth of invasion predicted disease-specific death independently of T and N stage (HR 1.31). Adding 5 mm and 10 mm depth cut-offs upstaged a third of patients and separated risk better: 5-year disease-specific death rose from 4% (T1) to 37% (T4). Practical point: always measure and report depth in millimetres.

cards.head: Pulling teeth after radiotherapy: jaw ORN in about 6%
cards.rib: Do a full dental check and needed extractions before radiation.
cards.take: A systematic review of 9 studies covering 462 irradiated head and neck patients found that tooth extraction after radiotherapy led to jaw osteoradionecrosis in 5.8%, mostly in the mandible; only 3 cases were in the maxilla. Patients who developed ORN had received a mean 68 Gy. Evidence on antibiotic cover was conflicting. Practical point: finish needed extractions before radiotherapy and avoid them afterwards where possible.

cards.head: Fibula harvest rarely leaves a wobbly ankle or a limp
cards.rib: Record ankle stability and gait at follow-up to catch problems.
cards.take: A systematic review of 32 studies covering 1,163 patients and 955 fibula flaps for head and neck reconstruction, assessed at a mean of 35 months, found ankle instability in 3.3% and gait disturbance in 5.5%. Assessment methods varied widely, so problems may be underreported. Practical point: reassure patients that lasting walking problems are uncommon, but check leg function at follow-up.

cards.head: After TORS, 50 Gy works for intermediate-risk HPV cancer
cards.rib: Phase II result: discuss 50 Gy rather than 60 Gy in MDT.
cards.take: In the ECOG-ACRIN E3311 phase II trial, 495 patients with HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer had transoral surgery, then treatment by pathology risk. Two-year progression-free survival was 96.9% with observation (low risk), 94.9% with 50 Gy and 96.0% with 60 Gy (intermediate risk), and 90.7% with 66 Gy plus weekly cisplatin (high risk). Practical point: 50 Gy looks safe after good surgery, pending phase III proof.

cards.head: Internal jugular system drains flaps better than the EJV
cards.rib: Use the external jugular as a backup, not the first-choice vein.
cards.take: In 151 head and neck free flaps by one surgeon, venous drainage into the internal jugular system, mostly via the common facial vein or end-to-side, succeeded in 99%, versus 92% with the external jugular vein (p = 0.03). All five venous clots were in the external jugular group. Urgent revision rescued five of six failing flaps. Practical point: prefer the internal jugular system when available.

cards.head: Flap clots strike early: 80% within the first 2 days
cards.rib: Arterial trouble shows early; keep checking veins from day two.
cards.take: In 990 free flaps at MD Anderson, pedicle thrombosis occurred in 5.1% and flaps were lost in 3.2%. Eighty percent of clots formed within 2 days; 90% of arterial-only clots appeared by the end of day 1, while 41% of venous clots came later. No flap that clotted after day 3 was saved. Practical point: monitor most intensively for 48 hours, with continued venous vigilance.

cards.head: Many oral cancer resections leave close or positive margins
cards.rib: Plan wider cuts and assess the resected specimen intraoperatively.
cards.take: Reviewing eight publications, Dutch authors found 30% to 65% of oral cancer resections had inadequate (close or positive) margins; their own two academic centres reached 85%. Inadequate margins were linked to more local and regional recurrence, distant spread and worse survival. Differing margin definitions hamper comparison. Practical point: agree one margin definition with your pathologist and check the specimen during surgery.

cards.head: After a lost flap, a second free flap beats pec for function
cards.rib: Keep pec major as backup when another free flap is not feasible.
cards.take: MD Anderson reviewed 3,090 head and neck free flaps (2000–2012); 40 were lost (1.3%). Of 28 patients given a second free flap, 27 succeeded (96.4%). For mouth and throat defects, all second-free-flap patients had over 80% speech intelligibility and 87.5% ate without a tube, versus 42.9% and 25.0% after pectoralis major salvage. Practical point: in fit patients, prefer another free flap.

lines: had skip spread to level III/IV

cards.head: 1 in 6 tongue cancers skip straight to levels III–IV
cards.rib: Tongue skips levels; elective dissection should reach level IV
cards.take: MD Anderson reviewed 277 tongue cancers treated with glossectomy and neck dissection. In 15.8%, the only neck disease sat in level IV, or in level III with levels I–II clear. Such 'skip' spread means a dissection of levels I–III alone can miss nodes. For elective neck surgery in tongue cancer, include levels I to IV.

cards.head: EXTREME: cetuximab added to platinum-5FU extends survival
cards.rib: No immunotherapy option? Platinum-5FU-cetuximab is the standard
cards.take: The EXTREME trial gave 442 patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer platinum plus 5-FU, with or without cetuximab. Adding cetuximab raised median survival from 7.4 to 10.1 months (HR 0.80), progression-free survival from 3.3 to 5.6 months, and response from 20% to 36%. It remains the chemo backbone where immunotherapy is unavailable or unsuitable.

cards.head: Cetuximab with postop RT cut relapse but not deaths
cards.rib: Intermediate risk, HPV-negative: cetuximab-PORT is an option
cards.take: RTOG 0920 randomised 577 resected intermediate-risk patients (mostly HPV-negative) to postoperative IMRT with or without weekly cetuximab. Overall survival did not differ significantly (HR 0.81). Disease-free survival improved: 71.7% vs 63.6% at 5 years. Severe acute toxicity rose from 39.7% to 70.3%, but late toxicity was similar. Consider it only for selected, fit HPV-negative patients.

cards.head: After platinum fails, pembrolizumab beats second-line chemo
cards.rib: Platinum-refractory disease: offer PD-1 therapy over old chemo
cards.take: KEYNOTE-040 randomised 495 patients whose head and neck cancer progressed after platinum to pembrolizumab or investigator's choice of methotrexate, docetaxel or cetuximab. Median survival was 8.4 vs 6.9 months (HR 0.80). Serious treatment side effects fell from 36% to 13%. For platinum-refractory disease, a PD-1 drug is the better and gentler second-line choice.

cards.head: Saliva carries tumour DNA in every oral cavity cancer tested
cards.rib: Saliva suits mouth cancers, blood suits throat; not yet routine
cards.take: Johns Hopkins researchers searched saliva and blood of 93 head and neck cancer patients for tumour mutations or HPV DNA. With both samples, 96% were detected, including all 10 early-stage cases. Saliva found 100% of oral cavity cancers; blood worked better for throat and larynx. Saliva DNA also preceded 3 recurrences. Promising, but still research, not routine care.

cards.head: On a toothless jaw, cancer usually enters via the ridge top
cards.rib: Plan rim resections assuming entry through the alveolar crest
cards.take: Brown and colleagues studied how oral cancer entered the mandible in 100 consecutive patients. In toothed jaws, all 13 tumours entered where they touched the bone. In edentulous jaws, 23 of 42 (55%) entered through the occlusal ridge. Deeper, larger tumours invaded more aggressively. When planning a rim resection, assume entry at or below the ridge crest.

cards.head: Blood clots follow about 1 in 20 head and neck free flaps
cards.rib: Risk-stratify clot prophylaxis and balance it against bleeding
cards.take: A centre reviewed 949 head and neck free flap patients over ten years. Within 30 days, 4.6% developed a venous blood clot despite routine prophylaxis, mostly enoxaparin 30 mg twice daily. Clots were linked to higher BMI, lung disease and longer hospital stays. Major bleeding occurred in 8.7%. Risk-score patients, mobilise early and watch bleeding on anticoagulants.

cards.head: Taiwan's mouth screening of smokers and chewers saves lives
cards.rib: Target tobacco and areca users for regular visual mouth checks
cards.take: Taiwan has invited adult smokers and betel quid chewers to visual mouth screening since 2004; 2.33 million were covered and 55% attended. After correcting for self-selection, screened people had 26% fewer oral cancer deaths (RR 0.74) and 21% fewer stage III–IV cancers (RR 0.79). Simple visual examination of high-risk users works at national scale.

cards.head: Raising the ALT above the fascia spares the donor thigh
cards.rib: Keep the fascia intact when you can; the thigh heals kinder.
cards.take: A Taiwanese team compared 30 ALT flaps raised above the thigh fascia (suprafascial) with 31 raised below it. Flap success was almost identical, 96.7% versus 96.8%, with no difference in flap size, harvest time or complications. The suprafascial group had fewer odd thigh sensations and higher donor-site satisfaction. Practical point: if perforators are dissected carefully, suprafascial harvest gives a kinder thigh.

cards.head: ICG perfusion check in theatre linked to fewer flap losses
cards.rib: Use ICG, where available, to trim poorly perfused skin early.
cards.take: Eight studies with 2,179 free flaps compared checking flap blood flow with indocyanine green (ICG) dye during surgery against clinical judgement alone. ICG use was linked to 90% lower odds of partial flap failure, 41% lower odds of total failure and 53% lower odds of reoperation. Flaps were not all head and neck. Practical point: where available, ICG helps decide what to trim before inset.

cards.head: Forearm donor site: tendon shows in 8%, graft fails in 11%
cards.rib: Counsel patients: about 1 in 10 forearm grafts heal slowly.
cards.take: This 2026 review pooled 22 studies of radial forearm donor sites. Tendon exposure happened in about 8% of patients and skin-graft loss or failure in about 11%. No closure method, graft type or dressing proved better than another, and the evidence quality was low. Practical point: protect the paratenon, secure the graft well, and warn patients that some donor wounds heal slowly.

cards.head: Flap takebacks cluster in the first 2 days, fade by day 5
cards.rib: Watch hardest for 48 hours; ease off after the fifth day.
cards.take: US NSQIP data on 3,906 head and neck free flaps tracked when patients returned to theatre. The daily takeback rate was 0.95% on days 0-1, 0.54% on day 2, 0.26% on day 3 and 0.20% on day 4, then just 0.03% per day from day 5 to 30. Practical point: monitor most intensely for the first 48 hours and keep checking until day 5.

cards.head: Tubed ALT rebuilds the gullet: 91% eat without a tube
cards.rib: Prefer a later voice puncture for better speech after ALT tube.
cards.take: In 114 patients, the pharynx and upper gullet were rebuilt with a tubed ALT flap after total laryngopharyngectomy; 71% had prior treatment. Only 2 flaps were lost. Fistulas occurred in 9%, strictures in 6%, and 91% ate by mouth. Fluent speech came in 81% with a later voice puncture versus 41% with a puncture at surgery. Practical point: ALT is a dependable gullet substitute.

cards.ev: Meta-analysis · Br J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2024
cards.head: Scapular tip flap survives in 99% of head and neck repairs
cards.rib: Reliable bone for jaw and palate; expect minor wound issues.
cards.take: Twenty-three studies with 474 patients, most after cancer surgery, were pooled for the scapular tip free flap. Pooled flap success was 99%. Complications of any kind were common at 38%, and about 1 in 5 patients went back to theatre, but only 1.5% needed a new flap. Practical point: the scapular tip is a very reliable bone flap; plan for minor wound problems.

cards.head: Supreme Court slams hospital mark-ups on cancer drugs
cards.rib: Watch for the verdict; it may change chemo billing in India.
cards.take: Hearing a drug-pricing petition on 27 October, India's Supreme Court criticised hospital mark-ups, citing a chemotherapy injection bought for about Rs 11,000 and billed at Rs 1.3 lakh. The Centre's 30% trade-margin cap on anti-cancer drugs covers only part of the market, and about 90% of medicines sit outside price control. Verdict reserved. Practical point: drug costs may face tighter rules.

cards.head: Scapular tip costs arm function no more than a forearm flap
cards.rib: Choose by defect; arm function costs are mild for each flap.
cards.take: Twelve studies measured patient-reported arm disability (DASH score, 0-100, higher is worse) about 20 months after flap harvest. Scores were low and similar: radial forearm 12.1, scapular tip 12.2, serratus 16.5 and bony forearm 18.0, with no significant differences. Most data were retrospective. Practical point: shoulder-blade bone does not cost patients more arm function than a forearm flap.

cards.head: Survivorship clinic during RT linked to fewer relapses
cards.rib: Bring speech, diet and dental support in before RT ends.
cards.take: A single-centre retrospective study of 471 patients getting curative radiotherapy found that 148 who attended a same-day survivorship clinic (speech therapy, physiotherapy, nutrition, dental) before radiation ended had 55% lower odds of missing treatment. Their 3-year recurrence risk was lower (HR 0.62), as was the risk of relapse or death (HR 0.61). Not randomised. Practical point: start rehab support during treatment, not after.

cards.head: One forearm vein: deep system clots less, both work
cards.rib: Single vein? Favour the deep comitantes if outflow looks good.
cards.take: Six cohort studies covering 1,073 forearm flaps drained by a single vein were pooled. A superficial vein more than doubled the odds of venous trouble (OR 2.29) versus the deep venae comitantes, but those flaps were rescued more often and total loss did not differ. Practical point: with one vein, the deep system is a safe default; pick the best outflow.

cards.head: ICMR: tobacco drives 2 in 3 male cancers in Kamrup, Assam
cards.rib: Late stage dominates in the northeast; screen tobacco users early.
cards.take: ICMR registry reports covered on 29 October rank Kamrup Urban fourth in India for male cancer incidence (211 per lakh) and third for women (174). Tobacco-linked sites made up 66.9% of male and 40% of female cancers, and the mouth ranks among top male sites. About 74% of oral cancers were found at locoregional stage. Practical point: the northeast needs tobacco cessation and early oral screening.

cards.head: Free flaps for jaw ORN fail in only about 3%
cards.rib: Irradiated jaw is no bar to free flaps; refer advanced ORN early.
cards.take: Pooling 46 studies with about 1,300 free flaps used to rebuild the jaw after osteoradionecrosis, total flap loss was just 3.1% (95% CI 1.3–5.4%). Results varied moderately between centres, with no single explaining factor. Despite heavily irradiated, scarred tissue, free flaps proved dependable. Practical point: do not delay or deny free flap reconstruction for advanced jaw ORN out of fear of failure.

cards.head: Buccinator invasion marks buccal cancers that spread to neck
cards.rib: Look for buccinator spread on MRI; it argues for neck dissection.
cards.take: In 75 operated cheek cancers from Tokyo, 40% had neck node spread. When the tumour reached the buccinator muscle, 73% (24 of 33) had nodes, and 5-year disease-specific survival fell to 72% versus 98% without muscle invasion. Depth over about 2 mm predicted nodes. Practical point: if imaging or the specimen shows buccinator invasion, treat the neck and consider adjuvant therapy.

cards.head: ITF compartment resection: 31 of 52 T4b cancers disease-free
cards.rib: Offer surgery for low ITF spread; above-notch disease does worse.
cards.take: An Indian rural tertiary centre treated 52 T4b oral cancers reaching the infratemporal fossa with composite resection, ITF compartment clearance and adjuvant therapy. At a mean 2 years, 31 were alive without disease; 14 recurred in the ITF. Close margins, extranodal spread, spread above the sigmoid notch and posterior ITF disease predicted failure. Practical point: ITF disease below the notch is worth operating on.

cards.head: Clearing a positive frozen margin is not a true R0
cards.rib: Plan a wide first cut; treat re-cut margins as high risk.
cards.take: This individual-patient meta-analysis pooled 8 studies of early oral cancer. When a positive frozen section margin was re-cut to clear, local recurrence risk was still nearly three times that of margins clear first time (HR 2.9). Margins left positive fared worse (HR 3.8). Re-cutting gave only a trend towards benefit. Practical point: aim for a clean first cut; a revised margin counts as high risk.

cards.head: Obturator or flap after maxillectomy: similar life quality
cards.rib: Discuss both options; let defect and dentition guide the choice.
cards.take: A review of 13 studies (9 pooled) compared 206 patients rebuilt with flaps or grafts and 260 fitted with obturators after cancer maxillectomy. Quality-of-life, speech and chewing scores did not differ meaningfully; one small difference in activity scores was not clinically relevant. Studies were small and mixed. Practical point: choose by defect size, teeth left and patient preference, not by an assumed QoL gain.

cards.head: Implants in bone flaps survive 92%; radiation is the threat
cards.rib: Plan implants at reconstruction, before radiation, to keep them.
cards.take: This review pooled 42 studies, 1,084 patients and 3,636 implants placed in free bone flaps of the jaw. Overall survival was 92.2% at a median 3 years. Implants survived 95.3% without radiotherapy but 84.6% with it, a nearly fivefold rise in failure risk. Implants placed at the primary surgery did well (97%). Practical point: place implants before radiotherapy when feasible.

cards.head: Pec major flap: zero total losses in 224 oral repairs
cards.rib: Keep pec major for soft tissue; use free bone for the front jaw.
cards.take: A Rotterdam series of 224 pectoralis major flaps for mouth and throat defects had no complete flap losses and only 2% needed return to theatre, though 53% had some flap-related complication. Plates under the flap were removed in 66% of front-jaw defects but 22% at the side. Practical point: pec major is dependable for soft tissue, not anterior jaw.

cards.head: PNI in early node-negative oral cancer: PORT helps
cards.rib: Discuss PORT even in pN0 early oral cancer when PNI is present
cards.take: A 2025 meta-analysis pooled 7 retrospective studies (522 patients) with T1–T2, node-negative oral cancer showing perineural invasion. Those given postoperative radiotherapy had better 5-year overall survival (88% vs 77%), 5-year disease-free survival (86% vs 55%) and 3-year local control (89% vs 72%). The data are retrospective, but perineural invasion alone should prompt a PORT discussion at tumour board.

cards.head: Petosemtamab plus pembrolizumab: median survival 28 months
cards.rib: Promising but single-arm; await full LiGeR-HN1 phase 3 data
cards.take: Company-reported phase 2 update for ESMO 2026: 43 evaluable patients with PD-L1-positive recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer given first-line petosemtamab (a bispecific antibody) plus pembrolizumab had a 63% response rate (19% complete) and median overall survival of 28.2 months after 25.5 months' median follow-up. Rash and infusion reactions were common. Small single-arm data; await full phase 3 results.

cards.head: Nimotuzumab added to weekly cisplatin-RT improved control
cards.rib: Consider nimotuzumab when you must give weekly low-dose cisplatin
cards.take: In a Tata Memorial phase 3 trial of 536 patients with locally advanced head and neck cancer, adding weekly nimotuzumab to radiotherapy with weekly cisplatin 30 mg/m² lowered the risk of progression by 31% (HR 0.69) and of locoregional failure by 33% (HR 0.67). Overall survival trended better but was not significant. Mucositis rose (67% vs 56%). A useful add-on when weekly cisplatin is chosen.

cards.head: Arterial couplers work in selected vessels; 1.9% clot
cards.rib: Evidence is weak; switch to sutures if the coupler won't fit
cards.take: A systematic review of 15 case series covering 395 attempted arterial couplings in free flaps found the device had to be abandoned for hand-sewn sutures in 8.4% of attempts. Among successful couplings, thrombosis occurred in 1.9% and device rupture in 0.3%, with coupling taking 4–10 minutes. All studies carried high risk of bias, so use arterial couplers selectively and keep sutures ready.

cards.head: Prior RT and neck dissection: in-field free flaps still work
cards.rib: Scan for usable in-field vessels before going to distant ones
cards.take: A multi-institutional review of 72 free flaps in 68 patients who had already received radiotherapy and neck dissection on the same side found 94.4% complete success, one total loss (1.4%) and three partial losses. Facial, external carotid and superior thyroid arteries were used most. After a previous free flap the facial artery was rarely usable (7% vs 67%), so plan alternatives in advance.

cards.head: Pre-RT extractions double jaw ORN; mean jaw dose matters
cards.rib: Plan dental clearance early and ask for a low mean mandible dose
cards.take: A Danish cohort of 1,224 patients given 66–68 Gy, mostly with IMRT, found jaw osteoradionecrosis in 4.6%, appearing at a median of about 11 months and 90% within three years. Surgery or tooth extraction before radiotherapy roughly doubled the risk (HR 2.09), and each extra Gy of mean mandible dose raised it about 4%. Finish dental work early and ask planners to spare the jaw.

cards.head: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab did not beat EXTREME first line
cards.rib: Dual checkpoint blockade isn't a first-line option outside trials
cards.take: CheckMate 651 randomised 947 patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer to nivolumab plus ipilimumab or the EXTREME regimen (cetuximab with platinum and 5-FU). Median survival was the same (13.9 vs 13.5 months). In CPS 20 or higher tumours it was 17.6 vs 14.6 months, missing significance. Severe side effects were far fewer (28% vs 71%). Pembrolizumab-based regimens stay the first-line standard.

cards.head: Fanconi anaemia raises head and neck cancer risk 500-fold
cards.rib: Favour surgery; radiation and chemo are poorly tolerated in FA
cards.take: In the International Fanconi Anemia Registry, 19 of 754 patients (3%) developed head and neck squamous cancer, a risk 500 times that of the general population, at a median age of 31. Surgery was well tolerated, but radiotherapy and chemotherapy caused severe toxicity and deaths. Half relapsed locoregionally and 2-year survival was 49%. Make surgery the mainstay and examine these patients' mouths regularly.

cards.head: UK SEND trial: elective neck dissection cut relapse
cards.rib: A second randomised trial agrees: don't just watch the N0 neck
cards.take: In the UK SEND trial, 250 patients with early, node-negative oral cancer were randomised to elective neck dissection or tumour removal with the neck watched. At 5 years, disease-free survival was 64.4% versus 50.9% (HR 0.66). Overall survival trended better (75.8% vs 67.6%) but missed significance because the trial closed early. It supports D'Cruz: treat the N0 neck upfront.

cards.head: Tongue DOI over 4 mm: dissect the neck; PORT added nothing
cards.rib: Depth over 4 mm calls for neck dissection, not routine radiation
cards.take: A US National Cancer Database study of 939 patients with stage I–II, node-negative tongue cancer looked at depth of invasion (DOI). When DOI was over 4 mm, elective neck dissection was linked to better overall survival (HR 0.37), but postoperative radiotherapy brought no survival gain at any depth. Registry data cannot prove cause. Let DOI drive the neck decision, not radiotherapy alone.

cards.head: Feeding by mouth within 5 days shortens free-flap stays
cards.rib: If swallow and wound allow, start mouth feeding in the first week
cards.take: A 2024 meta-analysis pooled 5 studies (1,097 patients) after free-flap reconstruction of head and neck defects. Starting oral intake within 5 days, versus later, did not raise fistula (RR 0.49, not significant), haematoma or seroma, or flap failure. Hospital stay was about 3 days shorter with early feeding. The studies were observational, but early feeding looks safe in well-selected patients.

cards.head: WHO 2020 update adds lichenoid lesions and GVHD to OPMDs
cards.rib: Name the lesion right; red patches and PVL need early biopsy
cards.take: A WHO Collaborating Centre panel refreshed the list of oral potentially malignant disorders. It keeps leukoplakia, proliferative verrucous leukoplakia (PVL), erythroplakia, submucous fibrosis, lichen planus, actinic cheilitis, reverse-smoker palate, lupus and dyskeratosis congenita, and adds oral lichenoid lesions and chronic graft-versus-host disease. Risk varies: about 1–2% for lichen planus, 30–50% for erythroplakia and PVL. Biopsy and follow red lesions closely.

cards.head: India launches 60-day Tobacco-Free Youth Campaign 4.0
cards.rib: Prevention is the cheapest oral cancer care; join local drives
cards.take: On 28 October 2026 the Union health ministry launched the fourth Tobacco-Free Youth Campaign, a 60-day national drive now centred on colleges and universities. It aims to stop young people starting tobacco, help users quit and tighten enforcement of tobacco laws. Earlier rounds declared over 5.8 lakh institutions and 73,000 villages tobacco-free. Head and neck teams can link clinics and campus talks to it.

cards.head: Fibula donor site: direct closure or graft heal alike
cards.rib: Let skin tension decide; both closure options heal comparably
cards.take: A small meta-analysis of 5 cohort studies (119 patients) compared closing the fibula donor site directly with covering it with a skin graft. Donor-site problems were similar (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.62–1.83). With so few patients the answer is not final. Practical point: close directly when the skin meets without tension, and graft rather than force a tight closure.

cards.head: ALT plus plate matched double flaps on plate exposure
cards.rib: Plate-only jaw rebuilds work, but expect more infection and pain
cards.take: A propensity-matched study of 62 patients with composite jaw defects compared an ALT flap over a bridging plate with bone plus soft-tissue free flaps. Five-year freedom from plate exposure was similar (47.4% vs 45.5%), as were flap loss and survival. But the ALT-plus-plate group had more wound infection (38.7% vs 12.9%) and worse pain scores. Choose bone when the patient can tolerate it.

cards.head: Gutka ban dodged by twin packs; Supreme Court seeks action
cards.rib: Ask about pan masala plus tobacco sachets, not only 'gutka'
cards.take: A 23 October report from Assam describes how the gutka ban is sidestepped: pan masala and flavoured tobacco are sold as separate sachets that users mix themselves, often near schools. Officials say shop-by-shop enforcement is impractical and want a nationwide policy. The Supreme Court has asked the Centre what it will do about twin packs. In history taking, ask about sachet mixing, not just gutka.

cards.ev: Landmark case series · Plast Reconstr Surg 1989
cards.head: 1989: the fibula flap that changed jaw reconstruction
cards.rib: Long, shapeable bone and two-team harvest made it the standard
cards.take: Hidalgo first reported the free fibula for mandible reconstruction in 12 patients with segmental defects averaging 13.5 cm, mostly after cancer surgery. Every graft had at least two osteotomies, yet all flaps survived and all bone cuts healed, including in 6 patients given postoperative radiation. The skin island was unreliable for mouth lining. Today the fibula is the jaw workhorse; plan skin perforators carefully.

cards.head: MRI finds jaw invasion better; CT better at ruling it out
cards.rib: Combine scans before choosing rim or segmental jaw resection.
cards.take: Pooling 16 studies (490 patients), MRI detected mandible invasion with 78% sensitivity and 83% specificity. Compared with CT, MRI picked up slightly more invaded jaws (not statistically significant) but gave more false alarms (significantly lower specificity). Practical point: an MRI-positive jaw may be over-called; combine CT, MRI and clinical findings, and confirm marrow status before choosing segmental over marginal mandibulectomy.

cards.head: Only major nodal spread (>2 mm) gains from adding chemo
cards.rib: Retrospective, but useful for sparing cisplatin in minor ENE.
cards.take: Across four high-volume centres, 755 node-positive oral cancers were re-read for spread outside the node. With minor spread (2 mm or less), adding chemotherapy to postoperative radiation made no difference: survival 57% either way in matched groups. With major spread (over 2 mm), chemotherapy raised disease-free survival from 11% to 33% and overall survival from 15% to 41%. Practical point: ask pathology to measure ENE.
