cards.head: Blood HPV DNA test spots throat cancer relapse accurately
cards.rib: Promising for follow-up; scans and biopsy still confirm relapse.
cards.take: Pooling 12 studies (1,311 patients) of a blood test that measures tumour HPV DNA after treatment of HPV-positive throat cancer, the test caught 86% of relapses and was correctly negative in 96% of patients without relapse. A positive result made recurrence about 25 times more likely. Methods are not yet standardised. Practical point: a rising result should prompt imaging and biopsy, not replace them.

cards.head: Cordeiro classification guides midface reconstruction
cards.rib: Classify the defect first; it decides bone, bulk and eye support.
cards.take: Cordeiro and Santamaria sorted 60 maxillectomy defects into four types, each matched to a reconstruction, mostly rectus or radial forearm free flaps, adding bone as needed. All free flaps survived. Of those assessed, 80% had normal or near-normal speech and 44% ate an unrestricted diet. Eyelid ectropion was common (71% of those assessed). Practical point: name the defect type to plan bone and soft tissue.

cards.head: Early buccal cancer: 28% hide neck nodes; dissect T2
cards.rib: Buccal cancer spreads early; do not watch the neck in cT2N0.
cards.take: In 101 patients with T1–T2 cheek cancer from international centres, 28% of node-negative necks that were dissected held hidden cancer. Neck recurrence cut median survival from 93 to 24 months and tracked with depth over 5 mm. In cT2N0 disease, elective neck dissection was linked to far longer survival (123 vs 26 months). Practical point: dissect the cT2N0 buccal neck, especially beyond 4 mm depth.

cards.head: EGFR/HER3 drug conjugate plus pembrolizumab: 58% respond
cards.rib: Small single-arm study; watch the blood counts and phase 3.
cards.take: At ESMO 2026, a phase 2 study in untreated recurrent or metastatic HNSCC tested iza-bren, an antibody-drug conjugate aimed at EGFR and HER3, with pembrolizumab. At the chosen 2.5 mg/kg dose, 58% responded (47% confirmed) and median progression-free survival was 8.5 months. Severe low neutrophils hit 30%; three treatment deaths occurred at the higher dose. Practical point: early signal only; phase 3 planned in China.

cards.head: 1 in 5 have nerve pain at the forearm donor site
cards.rib: Good donor-site wound care may prevent lasting arm nerve pain.
cards.take: In a multicentre survey of 114 patients after radial forearm free flap harvest, 18% reported nerve-type pain at the donor arm. Donor wound problems, mostly exposed tendons, affected 32% and were linked to this pain. Patients with nerve pain had poorer hand function and quality of life. Practical point: protect the paratenon, get reliable graft take, and ask about arm pain at follow-up.

cards.head: Best-of: transoral surgery and IMRT swallow equally well
cards.rib: Meeting data; dry mouth was worse early with radiotherapy.
cards.take: The phase III Best-of trial randomised 86 patients with early oropharynx, supraglottic or hypopharynx cancer to transoral surgery or swallowing-sparing IMRT. Swallowing at 12 months was similar (83 vs 86) and none needed a feeding tube. 2-year event-free survival was 84% with surgery and 72% with radiation; 36% of surgical patients needed postoperative radiotherapy. Practical point: both are valid; choose by expertise and patient goals.

cards.ev: Large case series · Plast Reconstr Surg 2002

fig.from: Wei et al, Plast Reconstr Surg 2002

cards.head: 672 ALT flaps: total loss in under 2%
cards.rib: The paper that made the ALT a soft-tissue workhorse flap.
cards.take: This landmark Chang Gung series reported 672 thigh flaps, 484 for head and neck. Total flap loss was 1.8% and partial loss 2.5%. Most skin vessels (87%) ran through the muscle rather than between muscles, yet only six flaps had no usable vessel. Practical point: be ready for intramuscular perforator dissection; it is the rule, not the exception.

fig.from: Dimovska et al, Plast Reconstr Surg 2025
fig.title: Scapula vs fibula, 120 patients

cards.head: Scapula matches fibula on face QoL with a kinder donor site
cards.rib: Add latissimus to the scapula for better lining and fewer leaks.
cards.take: Two Swedish centres compared 58 scapular and 62 fibular bone flaps for jaw reconstruction. The curved scapula needed fewer bone cuts for side-of-jaw defects. Facial quality of life was similar, but donor-site scores favoured the scapula. Taking latissimus dorsi with the bone reduced fistulas, plate exposure and non-union. Practical point: consider a scapula with latissimus for curved defects and patients with poor legs.

cards.head: Transverse cervical vessels: a safe backup recipient
cards.rib: Check the transverse cervical vessels before any salvage flap.
cards.take: Of 97 salvage or secondary free flaps in a Geneva series, 14 used the transverse cervical vessels when carotid branches were scarred or used up. None of these 14 had a vessel problem or flap loss, versus 10% microvascular complications with carotid branches. Minor haematomas and seromas were slightly commoner. They lie outside the old operative and radiation field. Keep them as your second-line recipient.

fig.title: Local recurrence risk ratio vs ≥5 mm

cards.head: Margins of 4–4.9 mm did as well as 5 mm in oral cancer
cards.rib: Retrospective data only; the true risk zone is 0 to 3.9 mm.
cards.take: Across 7 retrospective studies (2,215 patients), margins under 5 mm doubled the risk of local recurrence (RR 2.09). By millimetre, risk was highest under 1 mm (RR 2.96) and still raised at 1–3.9 mm (RR 1.8–2.2), but 4.0–4.9 mm margins behaved like 5 mm or more (RR 0.98, only 69 patients). Evidence is weak. Aim for 5 mm; treat under 4 mm as close.

fig.from: Walia et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2022

cards.head: After a lost flap, a second free flap succeeds in 93%
cards.rib: Don't default to a pedicled flap; plan the second free flap early.
cards.take: This meta-analysis pooled 429 head and neck patients whose free flap failed early. A second free flap survived in 93% (26 studies). Compared with a pedicled flap or wound care alone, the second free flap had 40% fewer perioperative complications (RR 0.60) and no longer hospital stay. Practical point: if the patient is fit and vessels allow, it is the most reliable salvage.

cards.head: Early blood ctDNA clearance flags who does well after CRT
cards.rib: Exploratory, unvalidated data; do not change treatment on ctDNA.
cards.take: An exploratory KEYNOTE-412 analysis at ESMO 2026 tracked tumour DNA in blood during chemoradiation with pembrolizumab or placebo. In HPV-negative patients on pembrolizumab, those who cleared ctDNA by cycle 3 had 73% five-year survival versus 39% in those who did not. Clearance also predicted outcome on placebo, so it looks prognostic rather than drug-specific. Practical point: promising for future trials, not yet routine care.

fig.from: Ramirez et al, Ear Nose Throat J 2025

cards.head: PENTOCLO healed or improved 9 in 10 jaw ORN cases
cards.rib: Cheap oral option; small uncontrolled studies, so audit results.
cards.take: A systematic review of 8 studies (141 patients, mostly mandible) assessed PENTOCLO: pentoxifylline, tocopherol (vitamin E) and clodronate taken for at least 6 months. 47% healed completely and another 43% improved markedly; full healing took about 10 months on average. Exposed bone shrank by 96%. Studies were small and uncontrolled. Practical point: offer it early in jaw ORN and plan for a long course.

cards.head: ZIP flap gives fixed teeth within a month of maxillectomy
cards.rib: Suits low-level maxillary defects; needs a prosthodontist early.
cards.take: Liverpool followed 35 consecutive patients with low-level maxillary cancer treated by the ZIP technique: resection, a soft-tissue free flap perforated by zygomatic implants, and a fixed bridge. Teeth were fitted at a median of 29 days, before radiotherapy in everyone who needed it. Flap survival was 100%, zygomatic implants 98.4% and prostheses 97%. Chewing scores were high. Consider it for low-level maxillectomy.

cards.head: Flap-reinforced closure cuts salvage laryngectomy fistula
cards.rib: Donor morbidity of a pec onlay is far less than that of a fistula.
cards.take: In 7 studies (591 patients) of total laryngectomy after failed radiotherapy, fistula rates were 31% with primary pharyngeal closure versus 22% when healthy tissue from outside the radiation field, a pectoralis major onlay or a free flap, reinforced the repair. That is about one-third lower risk (RR 0.63). Data are retrospective. Practical point: reinforce the pharyngeal closure routinely in salvage laryngectomy.

cards.head: Flap oximetry (NIRS) catches failure early enough to save it
cards.rib: Use oximetry as an add-on; never drop regular clinical checks.
cards.take: A review of 21 observational studies (3,662 flaps) compared two add-on monitors: near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) and hyperspectral imaging. Flap survival was 99.2% with NIRS versus 92.5% with hyperspectral imaging, and salvage of compromised flaps 88% versus 22%. There were no randomised trials and no cost data. Practical point: oximetry adds early warning, but clinical checks remain the gold standard.

cards.head: Cisplatin-free pembrolizumab larynx regimen misses target
cards.rib: Small single-arm study; keep cisplatin-based larynx preservation.
cards.take: SMART-KEY, a 43-patient single-arm phase 2 trial from Brazil presented at ESMO 2026, gave stage III–IVB laryngeal cancer carboplatin-paclitaxel-pembrolizumab induction, then radiotherapy with pembrolizumab and maintenance. Two-year laryngectomy-free survival was 65%, not significantly better than the 59% historical benchmark; larynx preservation was 84%. Grade 3 or worse toxicity hit 42%, and six patients died of adverse events. Cisplatin chemoradiation stays standard.

fig.from: Vani et al, JCO Glob Oncol 2024
fig.title: HPV-attributable fraction in India

cards.head: In India, HPV causes very few mouth cancers
cards.rib: Test p16 in throat cancers; in mouth cancer HPV rarely matters.
cards.take: Across 34 Indian studies, HPV was found in 20% of head and neck cancers, but detection is not causation. Using active-virus markers (E6/E7 mRNA or p16), the HPV-attributable fraction was only 3–4% for oral cancer, about 10–13% for oropharynx and 10–12% for larynx. Practical point: tobacco and areca remain the main drivers of Indian oral cancer; a positive HPV test should not change its treatment.

cards.ev: Meta-analysis · Br J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2022
cards.head: Extra anticoagulation does not save flaps but bleeds more
cards.rib: A good anastomosis beats extra heparin; avoid therapeutic doses.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 8 studies covering 3,531 head and neck free flaps tested extra antithrombotic drugs on top of standard low-molecular-weight heparin. Added anticoagulation did not lower flap thrombosis or failure (RR 1.54, not significant). Therapeutic-dose regimens tripled haematoma or bleeding needing intervention (RR 2.98). Practical point: rely on sound technique and standard prophylactic LMWH, not extra anticoagulants, to protect the anastomosis.

cards.head: Amivantamab triplet shrank 77% of HPV-negative tumours
cards.rib: Promising for HPV-negative disease; wait for phase 3 OrigAMI-5.
cards.take: At ESMO 2026, the phase Ib/II OrigAMI-4 study tested subcutaneous amivantamab, an EGFR and MET antibody, with pembrolizumab and carboplatin first-line in recurrent or metastatic HNSCC with CPS 1+. Tumours shrank in 77% (17 of 22) of HPV-unrelated cancers, including 3 complete responses, but in only 2 of 7 HPV-positive cancers. Small early study. Practical point: watch the phase 3 OrigAMI-5 trial.

cards.ev: Meta-analysis · Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol 2020
cards.head: Level IV is rarely involved in node-negative tongue cancer
cards.rib: Clear levels I–III in cN0 tongue; routine level IV adds little.
cards.take: Pooling 11 studies (498 patients) of clinically node-negative oral tongue cancer, Shabtay and Ronen found level IV nodes involved in only 2.8% and skip metastasis was rare. The authors recommend elective dissection of levels I to III for selected cN0 tongue cancers. Practical point: a supraomohyoid neck dissection is usually enough; add level IV only when nodes are found or suspected.

cards.head: ITF clearance offers T4b cheek cancer a real chance of cure
cards.rib: Select T4b cases carefully; node and nerve spread cut the gains.
cards.take: In 54 T4b buccal or alveolar cancers reaching the infratemporal fossa, composite resection with compartmental ITF clearance gave 52% two-year locoregional control and 54% two-year overall survival. Seven of 22 relapses arose in the ITF; 16 patients spread distantly. Perineural invasion, positive nodes and tumour within ITF tissue predicted worse outcome. Practical point: offer ITF clearance with curative intent to selected T4b patients.

cards.head: Niraparib with radiotherapy alone proved too toxic
cards.rib: Small single-arm study; keep PARP drugs with RT inside trials.
cards.take: The phase II RADIAN trial (ESMO 2026, LBA46) added niraparib and dostarlimab to 70 Gy radiotherapy in PD-L1-positive locally advanced HNSCC. With cisplatin chemoradiation (17 patients), 1-year disease-free survival reached 88%, beating a 65% historical benchmark. In 17 cisplatin-unfit patients on radiotherapy alone, all had grade 3+ toxicity, two died of treatment and DFS gain was not significant. Practical point: keep this combination inside trials.

cards.head: Immunotherapy before surgery rarely delays the operation
cards.rib: Neoadjuvant PD-1 drugs are surgery-friendly; combos respond best.
cards.take: In 20 prospective trials (570 patients), anti-PD-1/PD-L1 drugs given before surgery produced a major pathological response in 30.7% and complete response in 15.3%. Pairing with chemotherapy (57.5%) or radiotherapy (75.5%) raised major responses,, and CPS 20+ predicted benefit. Surgical delay occurred in only 0.3% and grade 3+ toxicity in 9.7%. Practical point: fear of delay should not stop neoadjuvant protocols.

fig.from: Almangush et al, Br J Cancer 2018
fig.title: High tumour budding: pooled risk

cards.head: Tumour budding flags oral cancers likely to spread
cards.rib: A simple slide count that sharpens early-stage risk; request it.
cards.take: Budding means tiny clusters of cancer cells breaking away at the invasive front. Pooling 16 studies, six tongue-only, Almangush and colleagues linked high budding, usually five or more buds, to neck node spread (OR 7.1) and worse disease-free (HR 1.83) and overall survival (HR 1.88; 3.27 in early-stage disease). Practical point: ask pathologists to report budding; it sharpens risk in early tongue cancer.

cards.head: Petosemtamab plus pembrolizumab halved death risk
cards.rib: Company interim data only; judge it when full results are shown.
cards.take: Genmab reported first-interim topline results of the phase 3 LiGeR-HN1 trial in first-line recurrent or metastatic PD-L1-positive HNSCC. Adding the bispecific antibody petosemtamab to pembrolizumab cut the risk of death by half (HR 0.50) and tripled the odds of response (OR 3.17), regardless of HPV status. Company-reported; medians and toxicity not yet public. Practical point: a likely new first-line option; await full data.

cards.head: Tranexamic acid cut transfusions without clotting flaps
cards.rib: TXA seems safe with free flaps; randomised trials are still due.
cards.take: Among 397 head and neck free flap patients, a low-cost tranexamic acid protocol (185) was compared with historical controls (212). Blood loss fell from 264 to 196 ml and transfusion from 20.7% to 12.9%. Flap failure (2.7% vs 2.3%), vascular compromise, DVT and pulmonary embolism did not rise. Practical point: TXA looks safe in free flap surgery, but randomised proof is still awaited.

cards.head: Phone camera AI helps health workers triage mouth lesions
cards.rib: Use AI-assisted photos to triage; biopsy remains the final word.
cards.take: An Indian study screened 5,025 people with a smartphone dual-image device in hospitals and low-resource communities. Remote specialist reading matched on-site experts with 95% sensitivity and 84% specificity. Health workers alone caught only 60% of lesions, while the phone-based AI caught 82% and the cloud-based AI 87%. Pairing frontline workers with AI and teleconsultation makes community oral screening practical.

cards.head: Implants in irradiated jaws survive 82% vs 95% unirradiated
cards.rib: Place implants before radiation if possible; warn of more failure.
cards.take: An umbrella review pooled 11 systematic reviews covering 73,674 dental implants in head and neck cancer patients. Survival was 81.5% in irradiated bone (2,674 failures among 14,471 implants) against 94.6% in non-irradiated bone (1,825 of 34,092). The underlying studies were of limited quality. Implants remain feasible after radiotherapy, but counsel patients that about 1 in 5 may fail.

cards.head: India orders states to act on unapproved nicotine pouches
cards.rib: Steer quitters to approved nicotine replacement, not pouches.
cards.take: India's health ministry has directed states to search, seize and prosecute sales of unapproved oral nicotine pouches such as ZYN and White Fox, citing rising online and shop sales and risk to children. The national drug advisory board has advised that no new nicotine formulations be approved. Pouches lack Indian approval; licensed gums, lozenges and patches remain the legal quitting aids.

fig.title: Total flap loss by resident checks

cards.head: Hourly nurse checks matter; resident check timing did not
cards.rib: Invest in trained flap nurses; act fast when they call.
cards.take: Across 9 US centres, 1,085 head and neck free flaps had hourly nurse checks while residents checked every 4, 8 or 12 hours. Flap compromise hit 10% (105 patients); of 96 taken back, 46 were fully saved. Total flap loss did not differ by resident schedule: 4% (4-hourly), 6% (8-hourly), 3% (12-hourly). A trained, hourly nursing team is the real safety net.

cards.head: ORATOR: radiation edged robotic surgery on swallowing
cards.rib: Both work; choose by side-effect profile and patient preference.
cards.take: ORATOR randomised 68 patients with early (T1–T2, N0–2) oropharyngeal cancer to radiotherapy or transoral robotic surgery plus neck dissection. One-year swallowing score (MDADI) was 86.9 after radiation versus 80.1 after surgery, statistically but not clinically meaningful. Radiation caused more hearing loss and neutropenia; surgery more trismus and one bleeding death. Survival was similar; share both options.

fig.from: Jain et al, Oral Oncol Rep 2024
fig.title: 5-year overall survival

cards.head: Low masticator spread in buccal cancer is still curable
cards.rib: Map masticator spread on MRI; offer surgery for low-level disease.
cards.take: In 213 operated advanced buccal cancers from India, 5-year overall survival was 68% for pT4a, 43% when spread reached only the masseter or medial pterygoid, and 21% when it reached the lateral pterygoid or temporalis. Perineural invasion and extranodal spread also hurt survival, and adjuvant therapy helped. Low masticator involvement deserves radical surgery, not palliation.

fig.from: Vitkos et al, J Oral Maxillofac Res 2025
fig.title: Temporal recipient vessels: outcomes

cards.head: Temporal vessels: a dependable recipient site for free flaps
cards.rib: In a hostile neck, look up to the temporal vessels before grafts.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 21 studies (773 free flaps in 759 patients) used the superficial temporal vessels as recipients for facial and jaw reconstruction. Arterial clots occurred in 1.4% and venous trouble in 5.1%; 7.7% returned to theatre and total flap loss was 4.1%. Results resemble neck vessels, making the temporal pair a sound choice when the neck is scarred or irradiated.

cards.head: TPF before surgery did not improve oral cancer survival
cards.rib: Operate first on resectable oral cancer; induction is for trials.
cards.take: In a phase 3 trial, 256 patients with resectable stage III–IVA oral cancer received either two cycles of docetaxel-cisplatin-fluorouracil (TPF) before surgery and radiotherapy, or went straight to surgery. After a median 70 months, survival was no different between arms. Patients whose tumours responded well under the microscope did better, but routine induction chemotherapy before resectable oral cancer surgery is not supported.

fig.title: ITF compartment and outcome after NACT

cards.head: High ITF spread behind the maxilla carries the worst outlook
cards.rib: Map ITF compartments; pterygopalatine spread is a red flag.
cards.take: In 154 Tata Memorial patients with unresectable oral cancer given induction chemotherapy, low ITF disease and disease limited to the retroantral fat did equally well (p=0.692). Posterior high ITF spread did worse, and involvement of the pterygopalatine fossa or pterygomaxillary fissure was worst, with poor chemotherapy response (p=0.007). Map ITF compartments on imaging before promising resectability.

cards.head: Disruptive TP53 mutations shorten survival after surgery
cards.rib: A broken TP53 brake predicts worse survival, independent of stage.
cards.take: TP53 is the cell's 'brake' gene. In 420 surgically treated head and neck cancers, 53% carried a TP53 mutation. Mutations that wreck the protein's shape or binding raised the risk of death by about 70% (HR 1.7), even after adjusting for stage. Milder mutations had no clear effect. Not every mutation is equal; the type of damage matters.

cards.head: Only marrow invasion of the jaw worsens survival
cards.rib: Ask pathology for marrow status, not just 'bone involved'.
cards.take: Among 498 operated oral cancers, 102 invaded bone. Erosion limited to the outer cortex did not change overall or disease-specific survival after adjustment. Invasion into the marrow independently raised the risk of death (HR 1.9) and cancer death (HR 2.1), mainly through distant spread rather than local or neck relapse. Read the pathology for marrow, not just 'bone involved'.

cards.head: Scapula flap has the fewest late wound and plate problems
cards.rib: Follow bony flaps for 3 years; plate exposure often comes late.
cards.take: Across 617 bony free flaps followed at least 6 months (312 fibula, 230 osteocutaneous radial forearm, 75 scapula), the scapula had the fewest late problems. Compared with scapula, fibula had three times the odds of late wound complications and 2.6 times the odds of plate exposure. Late complications kept rising until about 3 years. Consider scapula when hardware exposure risk is high.

cards.head: Ulnar forearm flap leaves a kinder donor site than radial
cards.rib: Consider the ulnar side when donor-hand function matters most.
cards.take: In 55 head and neck patients, 28 had a radial and 27 an ulnar forearm flap. After radial harvest, 15% had a weaker hand, 14% lost skin graft and 18% disliked the scar. After ulnar harvest, none lost strength, 4% had partial graft loss and none complained about appearance. For thin soft-tissue defects, the ulnar forearm is a worthy alternative.

cards.head: Close margin means under 1 mm, not under 5 mm
cards.rib: Under 1 mm is the danger zone; 1–5 mm adds little extra risk.
cards.take: In 432 oral cancer resections, local recurrence was 44% with a positive margin and 28% when tumour lay under 1 mm from the ink. From 1 mm outwards, rates were similar: 17% at 1 mm, 13% at 2–3 mm, 11% at 5 mm or more. Cutting extra tissue after frozen section did not improve control. Treat under 1 mm as the true danger zone.

fig.from: de Bree et al, Clin Otolaryngol 2007
fig.title: Hospital stay

cards.head: Free forearm flap costs no more than a pec major flap
cards.rib: Free flaps give better function at similar cost to PMMC.
cards.take: Forty radial forearm free flaps were matched with pectoralis major flaps for similar oral and oropharyngeal defects. Surgery took longer with the free flap (692 vs 462 minutes), but hospital stay was shorter (24 vs 28 days). Two-year costs were about the same, roughly €50,000 each. Cost alone should not push you to a pec major flap.

cards.head: 54 Gy instead of 69.3 Gy eased swallowing in HPV cancer
cards.rib: Promising de-escalation signal; keep standard dose outside trials.
cards.take: A secondary analysis of two ECOG-ACRIN phase 2 trials (80 patients, HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer) compared 54 Gy with standard 69.3 Gy. At 6 months, the lower dose meant smaller declines in solid-food swallowing, dry mouth and voice. Severe mucositis was 30% vs 47%. Groups were not randomised against each other, so this supports trials, not routine de-escalation.

cards.head: India's own HPV vaccine Cervavac wins WHO prequalification
cards.rib: Cheaper HPV vaccine access may widen coverage, including boys.
cards.take: Serum Institute's quadrivalent HPV vaccine (types 6, 11, 16, 18), already approved by DCGI, is now WHO prequalified, so UN agencies can buy it. It is gender-neutral for ages 9–26: two doses at 9–14, three at 15–26. Approved uses are anogenital cancers; oropharyngeal protection is not claimed, though HPV16 drives most HPV throat cancers.

fig.from: Obayemi et al, J Surg Oncol 2019

cards.head: Elective neck dissection linked to better palate survival
cards.rib: Hidden nodes can't be predicted; weigh elective neck dissection.
cards.take: In 1,830 node-negative hard palate and upper gum cancers from a US national database, 422 had elective neck dissection and 14% of these had hidden nodes. No factor, including advanced T stage, predicted which necks were positive. Elective dissection was linked to better overall survival (HR 0.75), in both T1 and T4 tumours. Consider treating the N0 neck here.

cards.head: 60 Gy plus weekly cisplatin works for low-risk HPV throat
cards.rib: De-escalation keeps the cisplatin; 60 Gy alone missed the bar.
cards.take: NRG-HN002 randomised 306 non-smoking, HPV-positive oropharynx cancer patients to a reduced 60 Gy dose. With weekly cisplatin, 2-year progression-free survival was 90.5% and swallowing scores stayed good; 60 Gy alone gave 87.3% and missed the trial's 85% bar. This is phase II proof, so use the lighter dose only within trials or protocols.

cards.head: Early oral cancer over 4 mm deep needs a neck dissection
cards.rib: Depth over 4 mm (less in tongue) tips the balance to the neck.
cards.take: In 222 pT1-T2 oral cancers from Rotterdam, 23.5% of elective neck dissections found hidden nodes. Each extra millimetre of depth raised the odds by 30%, and risk passed 20% at about 4.3 mm; in the tongue the threshold fell to 3-4 mm. Measure depth of invasion carefully and treat the neck once it exceeds 4 mm.

cards.head: Weekly docetaxel boosts survival when cisplatin is unsafe
cards.rib: Cisplatin-unfit? Offer low-dose weekly docetaxel with radiation.
cards.take: Tata Memorial randomised 356 locally advanced head and neck cancer patients who could not take cisplatin. Adding docetaxel 15 mg/m² weekly to radiotherapy raised 2-year disease-free survival from 30.3% to 42% and overall survival from 41.7% to 50.8%. Severe mucositis and dysphagia rose, so plan nutrition and pain support from day one.

cards.ev: Systematic review · Br J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2017
cards.head: Fibula leads jaw rebuilds with 3.4% flap failure
cards.rib: Fibula is the safe workhorse; iliac crest trades risk for teeth.
cards.take: Brown's 25-year review pooled 9,499 bony jaw reconstructions. Fibula made up 6,178 of them; fibula, radial and scapula flaps failed in 3.4%, against 6.2% for iliac crest. Iliac crest more often carried implant-retained teeth (44% vs 26%). Non-union, fistula and osteotomy details were poorly reported, so audit your own outcomes in a standard way.

fig.title: Jaw ORN incidence by risk group

cards.head: Jaw ORN strikes 1 in 8 high-risk patients after radiation
cards.rib: Flag high-risk mouths before RT and get dental care done early.
cards.take: Princess Margaret followed 2,732 irradiated head and neck patients: 8% developed jaw osteoradionecrosis. Risk was 12.7% in those with oral or oropharynx primaries, mouth dose of 60 Gy or more, smoking, or advanced gum disease, versus 3.1% without. The team proposed ClinRad, grading ORN by how deep the bone necrosis goes and whether bone is exposed.

cards.head: A year of atezolizumab after treatment did not help
cards.rib: After curative treatment, follow up closely; skip a PD-L1 drug.
cards.take: IMvoke010 randomised 406 high-risk patients who had finished surgery or chemoradiation to atezolizumab or placebo for a year. Event-free survival was unchanged (hazard ratio 0.94), and 2-year overall survival was 82.0% versus 79.2%, not a real difference. Maintenance immunotherapy after curative treatment should not be offered outside trials; focus on surveillance.

fig.from: Machiels et al, KEYNOTE-412, Lancet Oncol 2024
fig.title: 24-month event-free survival

cards.head: Pembrolizumab with chemoradiation did not cut relapses
cards.rib: Keep immunotherapy off chemoradiation outside of clinical trials.
cards.take: KEYNOTE-412 gave 804 patients with high-risk, unresected locally advanced head and neck cancer chemoradiation plus pembrolizumab or placebo. Two-year event-free survival was 63% versus 56%, but the hazard ratio of 0.83 missed statistical significance, and 3-year survival was similar (72% vs 70%). Cisplatin chemoradiation alone remains the standard for unresected disease.

fig.from: Ahmadi et al, J Reconstr Microsurg 2017
fig.title: End-to-side vs end-to-end (risk ratio)

cards.head: End-to-end or end-to-side: flap survival is the same
cards.rib: Pick the join that fits the vessels; neither saves more flaps.
cards.take: A meta-analysis compared end-to-end with end-to-side joins in free flaps. For veins, end-to-side did not change clot risk (risk ratio 1.30) or flap failure (1.50); for arteries both ratios were about 1.04, and none reached significance. Choose the technique that suits the vessels in front of you, such as size mismatch or a precious jugular.

cards.head: Level IIb rarely involved in early non-tongue oral cancer
cards.rib: Sparing IIb protects the accessory nerve; keep it for tongue.
cards.take: Across 22 studies (2,001 oral cancer patients), level IIb held disease in only 6% overall and 7% of tongue cancers. Isolated IIb disease appeared in just 3 patients; it almost always came with level IIa nodes. The authors advise skipping IIb in T1–T2 non-tongue cancers, but clearing it for tongue primaries and whenever IIa or several levels are involved.

cards.head: Bilateral neck dissection raises tracheostomy odds 9-fold
cards.rib: Use a risk score; avoid routine tracheostomy for small defects.
cards.take: In 26 studies (27,029 flap reconstructions), about 42% of patients got a tracheostomy once routine-use series were excluded. Strongest predictors: bilateral neck dissection (OR 9.4), T3–T4 tumours (OR 3.9) and oropharyngeal site (OR 2.3); free versus pedicled flap made no difference. Tracheostomy complications reached 16%, with chest infection in 8%. Select patients by risk, not routine.

cards.head: Brush cytology is the most accurate add-on for oral lesions
cards.rib: Biopsy any suspicious lesion; adjuncts only help triage.
cards.take: For visible mouth lesions, a Cochrane review of 41 studies compared add-on tests against biopsy. Brush cytology did best (sensitivity 91%, specificity 91%). Toluidine blue staining caught 84% but gave 30% false alarms; light-based devices caught 91% but specificity was only 58%. All evidence carried high risk of bias, so none replaces a scalpel biopsy of a suspicious lesion.

fig.from: Smith et al, Surg Radiol Anat 2017

cards.head: 1 in 20 thighs has no usable ALT skin perforator
cards.rib: Have a plan B: the other thigh or a different flap.
cards.take: Pooling 23 studies covering 1,251 thighs, the mean number of ALT perforators ranged from 1.15 to 4.26, mostly running through muscle from the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery. About 5.4% of thighs had no skin perforator at all. Two veins usually accompany the pedicle. Map perforators before surgery and keep a backup flap planned.

cards.head: Vessel-depleted neck: flap loss only 2% with planning
cards.rib: Map a reliable vein before surgery; arteries are easier.
cards.take: A review of 57 studies, including 925 vessel-depleted necks after radical dissection or radiotherapy, found free flaps still succeed: flap loss was 2% and complications 11%. ALT (30%) and radial forearm (24%) were the usual flaps. Among 26 arterial and 31 venous options, superficial temporal artery (20%) and vein (18.5%) were used most. Secure the vein first; it decides success.

fig.title: Scapular free flap at a glance

cards.head: Scapular free flap: 2% failure across 1,447 flaps
cards.rib: Think scapula when fibula is unusable or soft tissue need is big.
cards.take: Pooling 110 studies and 1,447 scapular free flaps, failure was just 2% (95% CI 1–4%). Most flaps (89%) went to the head and neck, mainly after cancer surgery. Average bone was 7.2 cm long and skin paddles about 134 cm²; osteocutaneous and chimeric designs were common. A dependable option when you need bone plus a large, independently movable skin paddle.

cards.head: Prior radiotherapy nearly doubles free flap failure odds
cards.rib: Counsel irradiated patients on higher risk; plan vessels early.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 37 studies (12,408 patients, 12,668 free flaps) found overall flap success of 94.4%. Patients irradiated before surgery had higher odds of total flap failure (OR 1.80), partial failure (OR 1.90) and postoperative complications (OR 2.22). Radiotherapy does not rule out a free flap, but choose healthy recipient vessels carefully and watch these flaps closely.

cards.ev: Biomechanical study · J Bone Joint Surg Am 2000
cards.head: Plating the radius restores strength after bone harvest
cards.rib: Plate the radius whenever you harvest bone with a forearm flap.
cards.take: In cadaver forearms with an 8 cm bone segment removed, as for an osteocutaneous radial forearm flap, the intact radius was 5.7 times stronger in twisting and 4.2 times in bending. Adding a plate made the cut radius 4.0 times stronger in twisting and 2.7 times in bending than leaving it unplated. Prophylactic plating is a simple way to prevent donor fractures.

cards.head: Cisplatin mouth patch cleared early oral lesions in 21 of 22
cards.rib: Promising early data only; keep excising invasive lesions.
cards.take: Company-reported interim data (Privo, 5 October) from the phase 2 part of the CLN-004 trial: a cisplatin-releasing patch stuck on carcinoma in situ or high-grade dysplasia gave complete pathological response in 95.5% of 22 patients. No serious side effects; no recurrences at median 14 months. Small, early and non-randomised; not for invasive cancer, and surgery stays standard.

fig.from: Inamochi et al, Support Care Cancer 2026

cards.head: 5% weight loss before postop CRT: 2.5× relapse risk
cards.rib: Track weight after surgery; act before 5% is lost.
cards.take: A Tokyo cohort of 105 high-risk patients given surgery and postoperative chemoradiation with structured nutrition support, published 28 September, found median weight loss of 4.8% before chemoradiation. Those who lost 5% or more had worse relapse-free and overall survival (hazard ratio 2.54 for relapse). Weigh patients weekly after surgery and escalate feeding early.

cards.ev: NCDB cohort · Am J Clin Oncol 2021

fig.from: Xiang et al, Am J Clin Oncol 2021

cards.head: A single positive node may be enough to justify PORT
cards.rib: Registry data, not a trial, but pN1 alone deserves a PORT talk.
cards.take: In 5,800 surgically treated oral cavity cancers in the US National Cancer Database, only 35% of pN1 patients got postoperative radiotherapy. Those who did had better survival (adjusted hazard ratio 0.66). Without radiotherapy, pN1 patients fared like pN2; with it, they fared like pN0. Treat a lone positive node as a reason to discuss adjuvant radiotherapy, not to observe.

cards.head: Palate and upper gum cancers hide neck nodes in 1 in 5
cards.rib: Add elective neck dissection to maxillectomy for cN0 palate SCC.
cards.take: Pooling 29 studies, Chia and colleagues found that 22.2% of clinically node-negative hard palate and upper alveolus cancers had hidden neck metastases. Elective neck dissection cut regional recurrence by about two-thirds (relative risk 0.36). These maxillary tumours are not the low-risk neck we once thought. Plan an elective neck dissection alongside the maxillectomy, even with a clinically clean neck.

fig.from: Bui et al, Plast Reconstr Surg 2007
fig.title: Salvage after pedicle clot

cards.head: Re-explore a failing flap within 4 hours to save it
cards.rib: Do not wait for theatre slots: speed decides flap salvage.
cards.take: Of 1,193 free flaps at one centre, about 6% needed urgent return to theatre, mostly for pedicle clots (53%) or bleeding (30%). Vein clots were nearly three times commoner than artery clots and easier to save (71% vs 40%). Flaps re-explored within 4 hours of detection did better than those after 9 hours. Overall survival was 98.8%. Act fast at the first warning sign.

fig.from: Liu et al, Int J Implant Dent 2023
fig.title: Implant survival in fibula

cards.head: Implants at fibula surgery last as well as delayed ones
cards.rib: Consider implants at the index fibula surgery to save months.
cards.take: Seven studies (186 patients) compared dental implants placed in the fibula at the time of jaw reconstruction with implants placed later. Survival was the same: 93.3% (194 of 208) primary versus 93.4% (214 of 229) secondary. Infection was 17.3% versus 23.1%, not significantly different. Placing implants at the first operation can shorten the road to teeth without costing implant survival.

fig.from: Lakhiani et al, J Reconstr Microsurg 2016
fig.title: Thigh donor-site problems (range)

cards.head: Thigh flap donor sites heal well; numbness is the main cost
cards.rib: Counsel ALT patients about thigh numbness; weakness is rare.
cards.take: A pooled review of 116 articles and 4,554 thigh flaps, including the ALT, found donor-site problems were uncommon. Numbness was the most frequent, reported in up to 36% of patients; wound breakdown, contour dents, pain and seroma were each under about 8%. Only rectus femoris harvest measurably weakened the leg, by 21%. Warn patients mainly about lateral thigh numbness.

cards.head: Name mandible defects by the four corners they lose
cards.rib: Record the Brown class in op notes to plan and compare flaps.
cards.take: Brown and colleagues reviewed 167 reports and built a simple mandible defect code around four corners: both angles and both canines. Class I is lateral, II a hemimandibulectomy, III anterior, IV extensive; add 'c' when the condyle goes. Higher classes meant larger defects, more bone osteotomies and poorer function and looks. Use it to plan bone segments and to report outcomes in a common language.

cards.head: Infranotch T4b oral cancer behaves like T4a
cards.rib: Infranotch disease deserves radical ITF clearance, not palliation.
cards.take: This meta-analysis pooled 16 studies (11,790 patients) of oral cancers reaching the infratemporal fossa below the sigmoid notch. After surgery, 5-year overall survival was 53.2% and disease-specific survival 68%. Survival, disease-free survival and local control did not differ significantly from T4a disease. Infranotch tumours are resectable with compartmental ITF clearance and should be treated with curative intent.

cards.head: Laser therapy for mucositis cut opioid need during CRT
cards.rib: Low-level laser is a cheap, useful add-on for mucositis pain.
cards.take: In an AIIMS Raipur randomised trial (meeting abstract) of 82 oral cancer patients on chemoradiation, photobiomodulation started at grade 2 mucositis lowered pain from week 3 and painkiller steps from week 2. Only 4.9% needed strong opioids versus 14.6% with standard care. Radiotherapy breaks fell from 29.3% to 12.2%, a trend that missed significance (p=0.057).

fig.title: Early buccal: surgery vs surgery + RT

cards.head: Early buccal cancer: routine postop RT not proven to help
cards.rib: Give RT for adverse features, not merely for a buccal subsite.
cards.take: This systematic review screened 1457 studies and found only five retrospective cohorts (733 patients) comparing surgery alone with surgery plus radiotherapy for stage I-II buccal cancer. Adding radiotherapy did not improve overall survival (p=0.70) or locoregional recurrence (p=0.72). Evidence is thin and biased, so decide on adjuvant RT by margins, depth and nodes, not by subsite alone.

fig.from: Zhang et al, Cancer Prev Res 2012
fig.title: 5-year progression to cancer by LOH risk

cards.head: Chromosome losses predict which dysplasias become cancer
cards.rib: Mild dysplasia can still be high risk; follow it closely.
cards.take: In 296 people with mild or moderate oral dysplasia followed prospectively, lesions that had lost genetic material (LOH) at chromosome arms 3p or 9p carried a 22.6-fold higher cancer risk. Adding 4q and 17p sorted patients into groups: 3.1%, 16.3% and 63.1% progressed to cancer within 5 years. Low-grade dysplasia is not always low risk; molecular markers can flag it.

fig.from: Shen et al, J Reconstr Microsurg 2021
fig.title: Salvage success by day of re-exploration

cards.head: Flap salvage drops from 94% to 12% after day two
cards.rib: Hourly checks in the first 48 hours turn rescues into saves.
cards.take: Reviewing 109 studies and 44,031 free flaps, 5.8% went back to theatre and 2.1% were lost. Explored within 24 hours, 93.8% were saved; on day 2, 83.3%; on day 3, only 12.1%; after day 4, none. Venous problems caused 59.5% of failures and arterial 27.9%. Head and neck flaps failed in about 3%. Monitor most intensely in the first 48 hours.

cards.head: 4-week postop chemoradiation matched 6 weeks at 1 year
cards.rib: Await mature phase III data before shortening adjuvant RT.
cards.take: AIIMS New Delhi's randomised phase II HYPCON-2 (meeting abstract) treated resected high-risk head and neck cancer with cisplatin plus 50 Gy in 20 fractions (4 weeks) or 60 Gy in 30 (6 weeks). One-year locoregional control was 87.8% vs 84.2%, with better compliance and fewer severe skin, blood and mouth toxicities. Small, short follow-up; promising but not yet practice-changing.

cards.head: About 1 in 10 oral leukoplakias turn into cancer
cards.rib: Biopsy every white patch; watch dysplastic ones for life.
cards.take: Pooling 24 studies with 16,604 patients from 2015-2020, oral leukoplakia turned malignant in 9.8% overall, ranging from 1.1% to 40.8% between studies. Epithelial dysplasia on biopsy and a non-homogeneous (speckled or nodular) appearance marked the highest risk. Biopsy every leukoplakia, and keep non-homogeneous or dysplastic lesions under close, long-term review or remove them.

cards.head: Myofascial pec major leaks less than skin-paddle PMMC
cards.rib: Prefer myofascial pec or a free flap for pharyngeal patching.
cards.take: In 23 studies (794 patients) repairing partial pharyngeal defects after total laryngectomy, the classic pectoralis major myocutaneous flap leaked most: fistula in 34%, versus 17% for radial forearm, 10% for ALT and 7% for the muscle-only (myofascial) pectoralis flap. Strictures and flap loss were similar. If you choose pectoralis, the myofascial version is a reliable, low-fistula option.

cards.head: Compartmental and wide excision give equal tongue control
cards.rib: Clean 3D margins and en-bloc resection matter, not technique.
cards.take: Across four international centres, 933 tongue and floor-of-mouth cancers were treated by compartmental tongue surgery (113) or wide local excision (820). After propensity matching (98 vs 172), local-regional control was similar. Outcome hinged on depth of invasion, lymphovascular invasion and number of positive nodes, not the name of the operation. Aim for 3D clearance with en-bloc removal of the tumour-node tract.

cards.head: Reconstruction bar beats mini-plates for fibula mandible
cards.rib: Use a reconstruction bar unless you have a strong reason not to.
cards.take: Across 16 studies and 1,513 fibula mandible reconstructions, mini-plates had more plate-related complications than a reconstruction bar (32.5% vs 18.8%), plus more fistulas (15.8% vs 4.7%) and re-operations for vascular compromise (13.3% vs 4.0%). Infection and non-union were similar. Data are mostly non-comparative cohorts, but a bar is the safer default for oncologic mandible defects.

cards.head: Coupler for end-to-side vein joins is as safe as sewing
cards.rib: Mostly retrospective data; time saved is the real gain.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 40 studies (2,664 head and neck free flaps) compared coupler devices with hand-sewing for end-to-side venous anastomosis. Vein clots occurred in 2.5% with couplers vs 1.8% hand-sewn, and flap loss in 1.9% vs 2.5%; neither difference was significant. Couplers were clearly faster. Choose the technique you do best; the coupler mainly saves time.

cards.head: 24 hours of the right antibiotic is enough after free flaps
cards.rib: Pick the right drug first; longer courses add no protection.
cards.take: A meta-analysis of 5 studies (861 patients) having clean-contaminated head and neck surgery with free flap reconstruction looked at antibiotic duration. Once antibiotic type was accounted for, 24 hours or less was as good as longer courses (RR 1.09). The drug mattered more: clindamycin nearly tripled wound infection versus ampicillin-sulbactam (RR 2.85). Stop prophylaxis by 24 hours and prefer ampicillin-sulbactam over clindamycin.

cards.head: Sentinel-guided neck surgery matches elective dissection
cards.rib: Needs a trained team and lymphoscintigraphy to be done safely.
cards.take: A Japanese multicentre trial randomised 271 patients with T1-2, node-negative oral cancer to sentinel node-guided neck surgery or routine elective neck dissection. Three-year survival was 87.9% vs 86.6% and disease-free survival 78.7% vs 81.3%, meeting non-inferiority. The sentinel arm had fewer complications (9.0% vs 14.6%) and less neck stiffness. Where nuclear medicine support exists, sentinel biopsy is a valid option.

fig.from: Patil et al, Lancet Glob Health 2020
fig.title: Median overall survival

cards.head: Oral methotrexate-celecoxib beats IV cisplatin in palliation
cards.rib: A low-cost oral option when IV drugs are out of reach.
cards.take: At Tata Memorial, 422 patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer not suitable for curative treatment got weekly oral methotrexate (15 mg/m²) plus celecoxib 200 mg twice daily, or 3-weekly cisplatin. Median survival was 7.5 vs 6.1 months (HR 0.77), with fewer grade 3+ side effects (19% vs 30%). This cheap tablet regimen is a sound palliative choice where resources are limited.

rows: Extract at least 2 weeks before start
Limit jaw volume at 50 Gy or more
Root canal or filling over extraction
fig.title: ORN prevention and treatment: key actions

cards.head: ORN guideline: extract 2 weeks before RT, skip routine HBO
cards.rib: Stage ORN with ClinRad so all teams speak the same language.
cards.take: The 2024 ISOO-MASCC-ASCO guideline says any needed extractions should be done at least 2 weeks before radiotherapy, and planners should limit jaw volume getting 50 Gy or more. After radiation, prefer root canals or fillings to extraction. Give pentoxifylline 400 mg twice daily around invasive dental work. Routine hyperbaric oxygen is not advised; full-thickness ORN needs resection with free flap reconstruction.

fig.from: Lee et al (JAVELIN HN100), Lancet Oncol 2021
fig.title: 2-year progression-free survival

cards.head: Adding avelumab to chemoradiation gave no benefit
cards.rib: Chemoradiation alone stays standard for unresected disease.
cards.take: JAVELIN Head and Neck 100 gave 697 patients with locally advanced head and neck cancer standard cisplatin chemoradiation plus avelumab or placebo. The trial stopped early for futility: 2-year progression-free survival was 53% with avelumab vs 57% with placebo, and response rates were similar (74% vs 75%). Outside trials, do not add checkpoint drugs to definitive chemoradiation.

fig.from: Fowler et al, J Otolaryngol HNS 2022

cards.head: Oral cancer margins over 1 mm did as well as over 5 mm
cards.rib: Retrospective data; margin lost significance after adjustment.
cards.take: A Canadian single-centre retrospective study of 412 oral cancer resections compared margins. Against margins over 5 mm, those under 1 mm had double the risk of local recurrence (HR 2.01), similar to positive margins (HR 2.15). Margins above 1 mm did as well as over 5 mm. Treat under 1 mm like a positive margin; a 1-5 mm margin alone may not need more treatment.

cards.head: Cetuximab is no safer than cisplatin in HPV throat cancer
cards.rib: Cisplatin stays the partner for radiation in fit HPV patients.
cards.take: De-ESCALaTE randomised 334 patients with low-risk HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer to radiotherapy with cisplatin or cetuximab. Severe side effects were identical (4.8 events per patient in both arms). But cetuximab did worse: 2-year survival 89.4% vs 97.5%, and recurrence 16.1% vs 6.0%. Swapping cisplatin for cetuximab buys no comfort and costs cures; keep cisplatin for fit patients.

cards.head: Second-hand smoke kills 3.25 lakh Indians a year
cards.rib: Tobacco control at home matters as much as quitting in clinic.
cards.take: At a 2 October webinar marking 18 years of India's smoke-free public places rules, public health leaders cited Global Burden of Disease data: about 3.25 lakh Indian deaths a year from second-hand smoke and 444 million people exposed in 2023. They called for fully smoke-free public places with no designated smoking areas, and protection at home and work. Ask patients about smoke at home too.

cards.head: Routine ICU after free flap surgery does not save flaps
cards.rib: Reserve ICU beds for patients with airway or medical risks
cards.take: Eight studies with 2,349 patients compared intensive care with ward care after head and neck free flap surgery. Flap survival did not differ (risk ratio 1.46, not significant), nor did return to theatre, readmission or death. ICU patients actually had more pneumonia and sepsis. The studies were observational. A trained flap ward with regular monitoring can replace routine ICU stays.

fig.title: Median overall survival by RT start

cards.head: Start postop radiotherapy within 6 weeks of surgery
cards.rib: Book the radiation consult before the patient leaves hospital
cards.take: A US national database study of 25,216 patients with stage III-IV head and neck cancer looked at the gap between surgery and radiotherapy. Median survival was 10.5 years when radiation began within 42 days, 8.2 years at 43-49 days and 6.5 years at 50 days or more. Plan wound healing, dental clearance and radiotherapy booking early so treatment starts on time.

cards.head: Red patches and PVL carry the highest cancer risk
cards.rib: Grade dysplasia on biopsy and set follow-up by lesion type
cards.take: Ninety-two studies were pooled to see how often mouth precancers turn into cancer. Overall, 7.9% did. Risk varied widely: lichen planus 1.4%, lichenoid lesions 3.8%, submucous fibrosis 5.2%, leukoplakia 9.5%, erythroplakia 33.1% and proliferative verrucous leukoplakia 49.5%. Moderate or severe dysplasia had 2.4 times the odds of mild. Biopsy red and multifocal lesions early and follow them closely.

cards.head: Chewing tobacco: 84% of its deaths are in South Asia
cards.rib: Ask every patient about gutka and khaini and offer cessation
cards.take: A Global Burden of Disease analysis in The Lancet Global Health estimates 241 million people used chewing tobacco in 2023, causing 251,000 deaths. South Asia carried 84% of these deaths and had 14.6% adult prevalence. Chewing tobacco explained 17.3% of lip and mouth cancer burden worldwide and 30.5% in South Asia. India topped the country list for both men and women.

cards.head: Tongue cancer deeper than 7 mm often hides neck nodes
cards.rib: Measure depth on MRI or ultrasound before planning the neck
cards.take: MD Anderson reviewed 212 untreated patients with early cancer of the side of the tongue. One in four (26%) had hidden neck node spread. A depth of invasion of 7.25 mm best predicted these occult nodes, and 8 mm best predicted 5-year survival. Depth was an independent predictor of overall and disease-specific survival. Depth matters more than surface size when deciding on the neck.

cards.head: Adding nivolumab to postop chemoradiation cuts recurrence
cards.rib: Discuss adjuvant nivolumab for ENE or positive-margin cases
cards.take: NIVOPOSTOP randomised 666 patients under 75 with high-risk resected head and neck cancer, such as nodal spread outside the capsule or positive margins. Adding nivolumab to postoperative cisplatin-radiotherapy lowered the risk of recurrence or death by 24% (hazard ratio 0.76); 3-year disease-free survival was 63.1% vs 52.5%. Grade 4 toxicity roughly doubled (10% vs 5%). Survival data are not yet mature.

cards.head: Big palate defects do better with a free flap than obturator
cards.rib: Size the palatal defect first, then choose obturator or flap
cards.take: MD Anderson compared 113 patients after maxillectomy for cancer: 73 had a prosthetic obturator and 40 had free flap reconstruction. Speech and diet were similar for moderate defects. When more than half the palate was removed, free flaps gave clearer speech and a better diet. Recurrence was picked up equally well in both groups. Either works for smaller defects; prefer a flap for large ones.

cards.head: Infections cause 1 in 8 cancers; HPV ranks second
cards.rib: Advocate HPV vaccination in clinic and in public talks
cards.take: An IARC study in The Lancet Oncology estimates that 2.3 million new cancers in 2024, about 12% of all, were caused by infections. H. pylori (760,000) and HPV (750,000) led, followed by hepatitis B (360,000), Epstein-Barr virus (260,000) and hepatitis C (160,000). Over 75% occurred in low- and middle-income countries. Most of these cancers are already preventable with vaccination, testing and treatment.

fig.from: ICGC India Project Team, Nat Commun 2013
fig.title: Most often mutated genes

cards.head: Indian gum-cheek cancers carry their own gene fingerprint
cards.rib: Western gene data may not fit Indian tobacco-chewing patients
cards.take: India's cancer genome consortium sequenced gingivo-buccal mouth cancers from 50 patients and checked 60 more. Almost all (96%) used tobacco. Common faulty genes were TP53 (62%), FAT1 (44%) and CASP8 (36%), plus genes new to this cancer such as USP9X, MLL4 and ARID2. Tumours fell into three gene groups, some with longer disease-free survival. Chewer's cancer biology differs from Western head and neck cancer.

fig.title: Fewer than 18 nodes vs 18 or more

cards.head: Neck dissection yielding 18+ nodes linked to better survival
cards.rib: Use node yield as a quality check for every neck dissection
cards.take: In 572 patients from two RTOG postoperative trials, followed for a median of 8 years, finding fewer than 18 lymph nodes in the neck dissection meant worse survival (hazard ratio 1.38) and more local or neck recurrence (1.46). Distant spread did not differ. This is an association, not proof of cause. Aim for a thorough dissection and a careful pathology node count.

fig.from: Agha et al, J Reconstr Microsurg Open 2016
fig.title: Free flap failure rate

cards.head: Implantable Doppler lowers free flap failure
cards.rib: Add the Doppler to, not instead of, regular bedside flap checks
cards.take: Eight studies covering 3,801 free flaps compared the Cook-Swartz implantable venous Doppler with clinical monitoring alone. Flap failure was 2.0% with the Doppler versus 3.5% with clinical checks, a significant drop (odds ratio 0.37). In one series, compromise was spotted about a day earlier. Where affordable, use it as an add-on to regular clinical checks.

cards.head: Forearm donor site: full or split graft heal equally
cards.rib: Either graft works; pick by patient and surgeon routine
cards.take: Fifteen observational studies, with 933 radial forearm donor sites, compared closure with full-thickness versus split-thickness skin grafts. Neither major wound problems (risk ratio 0.43, not significant) nor minor healing problems differed. No randomised trials exist and certainty is low to very low. Choose the graft by patient factors and your own routine; full-thickness avoids a second raw donor wound.

fig.from: Chiesa-Estomba et al, Int Arch ORL 2023
fig.title: Marginal vs segmental: 5-year outcomes

cards.head: Marginal mandibulectomy is safe unless the marrow is invaded
cards.rib: Assess marrow invasion on imaging before choosing the resection
cards.take: Eleven cohort studies covering 2,023 patients compared marginal (857) with segmental (1,166) mandible resection for mouth cancer. Five-year local control and overall survival were the same. But when tumour had entered the bone marrow, segmental resection gave clearly better disease-free survival (hazard ratio 0.27). Keep the jaw rim when the marrow is spared; resect a segment when it is invaded.

cards.ev: Meta-analysis · Br J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2016

fig.from: Chen et al, Br J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2016
fig.title: ALT vs radial forearm for tongue (366 pts)

cards.head: Tongue: ALT works like forearm flap and spares the arm
cards.rib: Prefer a thin ALT for tongue when thigh fat allows
cards.take: Pooling 366 tongue reconstructions, 168 with the anterolateral thigh flap and 198 with the radial forearm flap, showed no difference in flap survival, complications, swallowing, speech or the look of the new tongue. The forearm donor site was worse, with more visible scarring and numbness. For hemiglossectomy defects, a thin ALT gives the same function while sparing the arm.

fig.from: Novakovic et al, Head Neck Oncol 2009
fig.title: Thrombectomy success

cards.head: Most flaps fail early; vein clots are easier to rescue
cards.rib: Re-explore a failing flap at once; early surgery saves flaps
cards.take: This review explains why free flaps fail and how to save them. Most failures appear within 48 hours, and venous clots are more than twice as common as arterial ones. Salvage succeeds in anywhere from 28% to over 90% of cases, with venous thrombectomy working in about 60% versus 15% for arterial. Monitor closely early and re-explore without delay.

cards.head: Specimen margin, not tumour-bed frozen, predicts recurrence
cards.rib: Check margins on the resected specimen, not just the wound bed
cards.take: In 406 patients operated for mouth cancer, local recurrence was 45% when the main specimen margin was positive versus 13% when clear. Tumour-bed frozen sections predicted recurrence less well (36% vs 19%). The specimen margin was the strongest predictor of recurrence. Orient the specimen and sample its margins directly, rather than relying on shavings from the wound.

cards.ev: Systematic review · Int J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2020

fig.from: Pucci et al, Int J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2020
fig.title: Flap ischaemia time

cards.head: Virtual planning cuts fibula flap ischaemia by 36 minutes
cards.rib: Use virtual planning for complex multi-segment jaw defects
cards.take: A systematic review compared computer-planned, cutting-guide fibula reconstruction of the mandible with free-hand shaping. Ischaemia time averaged 73.8 minutes with virtual planning versus 109.9 minutes free-hand, and total operating time fell by more than an hour, with better accuracy. Only six studies qualified. Use virtual planning for complex, multi-segment jaw defects where cost and lead time allow.

cards.head: Skeletonised pec major flap: 3.5% major complications
cards.rib: Keep pec major ready for salvage, unfit patients and bulky gaps
cards.take: A Chinese team used a slimmer, pedicle-skeletonised pectoralis major flap in 118 head and neck reconstructions in 114 patients. Major complications were 3.5%: two haematomas, one fistula and one partial edge necrosis. All patients were extubated and all but one resumed oral intake. The flap still earns its place for salvage, patients unfit for free flaps and defects needing bulk.

cards.head: OX40 drug plus pembrolizumab boosts responses in HNSCC
cards.rib: Early, company-reported data; await phase 3 survival results
cards.take: In the randomised phase 2 part of HexAgon-HN, 63 patients with untreated recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer (PD-L1 CPS 20 or more) got pembrolizumab with or without INBRX-106, an OX40 agonist. Response rate was 48.3% vs 26.5% and median progression-free survival 9.6 vs 4.9 months. These are company-reported interim results; survival data are pending.

fig.from: Liao et al, Ann Surg Oncol 2010
fig.title: 5-year distant metastasis

cards.head: Buccal vs tongue: same local control, more distant spread
cards.rib: Watch node-positive buccal cancer closely for distant spread
cards.take: In 863 operated patients from Taiwan, buccal and tongue cancers had similar 5-year local control (87% vs 85%) and disease-free survival (72% vs 70%). Buccal cancer had better neck control (87% vs 81%) but more distant metastasis (14% vs 8%), rising to 30% when nodes were positive. Node-positive buccal cancer deserves closer follow-up for distant spread.

fig.from: Frohwitter et al, J Craniomaxillofac Surg 2018
fig.title: Recipient vessels in the depleted neck

cards.head: No neck vessels? Internal mammary and cephalic rescue
cards.rib: Map backup recipient vessels before re-operating a treated neck
cards.take: This review of 26 studies covered 325 free flaps done in necks with no usable vessels after earlier surgery or radiation. Internal mammary (28%), transverse cervical (16%) and superficial temporal (15%) arteries were the commonest donors; the cephalic and internal mammary veins led for drainage. Complications occurred in 34.5%. Plan recipient vessels before surgery and keep these options ready.

cards.head: Jaw ORN after extractions around IMRT is uncommon
cards.rib: Extract hopeless teeth early, but don't delay radiotherapy
cards.take: This review pooled 875 patients who had teeth removed around IMRT for head and neck cancer. Osteoradionecrosis developed in only 3.2%. Extracting before radiotherapy appeared to carry less risk than extracting afterwards, but the data were weak and the authors found no conclusive proof. Keep pre-radiation dental assessment, remove truly hopeless teeth early, and avoid needless delays to radiotherapy.

cards.head: SBRT re-irradiation: less severe toxicity, same survival
cards.rib: Promising, but await full publication before changing practice
cards.take: In the randomised phase 2 SOAR-HN trial from MD Anderson, presented at ASTRO 2026, patients with recurrent head and neck cancer needing re-irradiation had either short-course SBRT over about two weeks or conventional re-irradiation over several weeks. At two years, grade 3 or worse toxicity was significantly more common with conventional treatment, while overall survival was similar. Full data await publication.

fig.from: Ahmadi et al, J Reconstr Microsurg 2014

cards.head: Two venous anastomoses cut flap failure by a third
cards.rib: Add a second vein when a good one is at hand and time allows
cards.take: Across 23 studies, free flaps drained by two venous anastomoses failed less often than those with a single vein. Flap failure fell by about 36% (risk ratio 0.64) and venous thrombosis by about 34% (risk ratio 0.66). The studies were observational, so judge each case. When a second good-quality vein is available and time allows, adding it is a sensible safety margin.

fig.from: Khayat et al, J Clin Med 2024

cards.head: Double-barrel fibula holds implants with 1.7% failure
cards.rib: Plan double-barrel fibula when implant-borne teeth are the goal
cards.take: A review of 17 studies (245 patients, 402 implants) looked at segmental mandible defects rebuilt with a folded, double-barrel fibula and then fitted with dental implants. Flap survival was 98.3% and only 1.74% of implants failed over a mean follow-up of 34 months. Folding the fibula gives more bone height for implants. Choose it when implant-borne teeth are a goal.

cards.head: ITF-involved mouth cancer: 1-year control only 37%
cards.rib: Low-ITF disease does better; counsel mid-ITF cases with care
cards.take: Twenty patients with T4b mouth cancer reaching the lower or mid infratemporal fossa had surgery with ITF clearance and then chemoradiation. Locoregional control was 74% at 3 months but fell to 37% at one year; one-year survival was 74%. Control was better when only the low ITF was involved (86% vs 40% at 3 months). Select patients carefully and counsel honestly.

fig.from: Salzano et al, J Clin Med 2025
fig.title: Scapular flap for the maxilla: pooled results

cards.head: Scapula flap rebuilds the maxilla with 2.6% flap loss
cards.rib: Small, mixed studies, but scapula suits complex maxillary gaps
cards.take: Pooling six studies of 231 patients, mostly cancer cases, the scapular free flap proved dependable for upper-jaw reconstruction. Total flap loss was 2.6%. Early complications occurred in 24%, fistula in 12% and donor-site problems in only 10%. Just over half (56%) had teeth restored and 52% returned to a normal diet. Keep it high on the list for complex composite maxillary defects.

cards.head: Cheap oral pills plus ultra-low-dose nivolumab beat IV chemo
cards.rib: Oral drugs plus ultra-low-dose nivolumab doubled 1-year survival
cards.take: Tata Memorial randomised 422 patients with advanced head and neck cancer needing palliative treatment. Oral methotrexate, celecoxib and erlotinib with ultra-low-dose nivolumab beat paclitaxel-carboplatin: median survival 10.3 vs 6.2 months, one-year survival 46% vs 23%, and fewer severe side effects. Most patients had mouth cancer, so this speaks directly to Indian practice.

cards.head: Swapping cisplatin for durvalumab failed in HPV throat cancer
cards.rib: Durvalumab can't replace cisplatin with RT in HPV throat cancer
cards.take: The CCTG HN.9 trial tested a gentler plan for intermediate-risk HPV-positive throat cancer: radiotherapy with the immunotherapy drug durvalumab instead of cisplatin. Cancer control was not better, and quality of life and swallowing were similar. Like earlier cetuximab trials, it shows de-escalation needs proof. Cisplatin with radiation remains the standard for fit patients.
